inputs: Public Form 5500 filings and available Schedule A/C records, employer size and plan-year information, employer-confirmed renewal dates and appropriately obtained business contact details.

Employer authorization, incumbent fee disclosures, plan documents, aggregate claims and pharmacy reports, stop-loss terms, underwriting requirements and privacy-controlled access to necessary participant information.

Licensed broker and specialist relationships, TPA and stop-loss proposals, captive participation terms, PBM rebate and spread definitions, NADAC availability and fallback pricing rules, and a $40–$65 PEPM service proposal.
operator_plays.mechanism: Use public Form 5500 Schedule A/C information, where filed and informative, to identify mid-market renewal and compensation-review opportunities, then offer an employer-authorized CAA 2021 service-provider fee-disclosure review. A properly licensed advisory team can seek broker-of-record appointments and compare bundled coverage with separately contracted TPA, stop-loss or suitable captive arrangements and a transparent pass-through PBM using an explicitly defined NADAC-based pricing methodology. Negotiate recurring $40–$65 PEPM advisory fees where supported by scope and client agreement, with all commissions and indirect compensation disclosed and no assumption that unbundling guarantees savings.
metrics: Recurring advisory revenue: enrolled employees multiplied by the contracted $40–$65 PEPM fee, less servicing costs and disclosed fee offsets.
Risk-adjusted employer cost: claims, administration, stop-loss premiums, pharmacy costs, collateral and runout obligations minus realized rebates and recoveries.
Service and retention quality: renewal retention, disclosure completeness, pharmacy guarantee reconciliation variance and unresolved participant access issues.
operator_plays.name: Mid-Market Level-Funded Benefits and Transparent PBM Advisory Operator

platform_risks.detection_metric: Adverse-scenario funding gap, claims-to-budget variance, unrecovered stop-loss balances and unexplained differences between disclosed and received compensation.
platform_risks.failure_mode: The proposed unbundled plan produces adverse claims exposure or undisclosed compensation despite appearing cheaper on headline premiums.
platform_risks.fallback: Retain or competitively rebid the existing structure when risk-adjusted economics are unfavorable, obtain explicit pricing fallbacks and narrow the engagement to disclosed advisory work until implementation conditions are satisfied.
platform_risks.impact: Employer costs exceed projections, coverage continuity deteriorates and advisory fees or the BOR relationship become disputed.
platform_risks.trigger: Incomplete claims data, stop-loss lasers or exclusions, nonrefundable captive collateral, ambiguous PBM rebate definitions or unsupported NADAC pricing for uncovered products.

workflow: 1. Analyze publicly available filings through permitted access methods, identify likely renewal opportunities and confirm current plan arrangements directly because filings are historical and may omit relevant compensation details.
2. Obtain employer authorization, review applicable CAA 2021 disclosures and existing termination terms, and define advisory deliverables and compensation before requesting any BOR appointment.

3. Compare fully insured and level-funded options using expected and adverse claims scenarios, stop-loss exclusions and lasers, captive collateral, TPA fees, pharmacy guarantees and rebates actually retained by the employer.

4. Implement the employer-selected structure with licensed parties, privacy safeguards and continuity planning; collect agreed PEPM fees and review total costs, disclosures and service performance at each renewal.

inputs: Customer authorization, three to four years of policies and premium audits, payroll registers, job-duty evidence, overtime breakdowns, officer election documents and subcontractor coverage records.
Applicable state classification rules, NCCI or independent-bureau worksheets, experience-period and valuation dates, carrier loss runs and documented claim corrections.
Carrier and bureau dispute procedures, policy-specific correction deadlines, a 30%–40% realized-refund agreement and licensed brokerage support for any BOR renewal engagement.
operator_plays.mechanism: Audit three to four historical policy years where carrier, state and rating-bureau correction rules permit, checking actual duties, payroll classifications, eligible overtime adjustments and officer exclusions or limits. Reconcile NCCI experience-rating worksheets, or the applicable independent bureau's equivalent, to accurate carrier loss reports and valuation dates; an open reserve is not an error merely because the ultimate claim later costs less. Recover documented premium overpayments for a negotiated 30%–40% contingency and pursue separately authorized, properly licensed BOR renewal work.
metrics: Realized premium recovery: received refunds and usable policy credits divided by audited historical premium, segmented by payroll, classification and experience-mod correction.
Correction conversion: dollars recovered divided by dollars submitted, alongside days from supported dispute to revised audit or bureau worksheet.
Renewal economics: separately disclosed brokerage revenue and verified prospective premium effect, controlling for payroll, operations, rates and coverage changes.
operator_plays.name: Workers' Compensation Classification and Experience-Mod Recovery Operator

platform_risks.detection_metric: Rejected correction dollars by reason, percentage of payroll supported by contemporaneous records and net premium change after the full audit.
platform_risks.failure_mode: A carrier or rating bureau rejects proposed corrections because classifications, loss valuations or retroactive deadlines were misinterpreted.
platform_risks.fallback: Withdraw unsupported claims, disclose any additional premium exposure, use the bureau's documented dispute process for defensible items and improve prospective payroll and claims reporting.
platform_risks.impact: No refund is issued, advisory effort is unrecovered and a broader audit may identify additional premium owed.
platform_risks.trigger: Unsupported separation of payroll, missing officer elections, treatment of later reserve reductions as historical errors or submission outside the permitted correction period.

workflow: 1. Map each policy to its governing state and bureau rules, establish the allowable correction window and reconcile audited payroll to contemporaneous employment and job-duty records.
2. Test class-code assignments, permitted overtime premium exclusions, officer elections or payroll limits and subcontractor treatment without relabeling work merely to obtain a cheaper rate.
3. Reconcile experience-mod inputs against losses reported for the applicable valuation date; submit evidenced payroll, classification or loss-data corrections to the carrier and bureau as required.
4. Obtain revised audits or rating worksheets, trace resulting premium credits through endorsements and receipts, collect the 30%–40% contingency and separately quote licensed BOR renewal services.

operator_plays.name: Private B2B Group Purchasing Organization (GPO) Umbrella & Contingent Spend-Audit Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Pool 10,000–75,000+ seats and indirect corporate spend across hundreds of SMB member companies under authorized master GPO volume brackets through Una, OMNIA or private vertical SaaS, parcel and telecom GPOs. Pair negotiated brackets with quarter-end vendor price-floor benchmarking informed by Vendr/Tropic playbooks, targeting 3%–12% vendor-paid administrative rebates and 25%–35% contingent Year-1 shared-savings splits under no savings, no fee agreements. Eligibility, rebate bases and benchmark access must be verified; disclose dual compensation and avoid double-counting rebates in client savings.
inputs: Executed GPO member and supplier agreements defining eligible aggregated spend, volume brackets, administrative rebates and compensation disclosures
Member-authorized invoices and seat inventories plus lawfully obtained, like-for-like Vendr/Tropic-style pricing benchmarks
Contingent audit contracts defining the Year-1 savings baseline, exclusions, 25%–35% fee schedule and independent reconciliation rights
workflow: 1. Enroll eligible SMB members with written authority and aggregate verified seat demand and indirect spend without exchanging competitively sensitive data.
2. Validate GPO purchasing eligibility and negotiate supplier volume brackets using lawful quarter-end benchmarks for comparable service and commitment terms.
3. Present disclosed vendor rebates and contingent fees, secure member approval and implement authorized contract changes against an agreed savings baseline.
4. Reconcile actual Year-1 savings and vendor rebates, charge only earned shared-savings fees and audit bracket eligibility and renewal pricing.
metrics: Verified eligible seats and annual member spend within contracted GPO brackets
Realized Year-1 member savings net of contingent fees on a normalized baseline
Collected administrative rebates and shared-savings fees net of reversals

chapters.question_prompt: How do fully insured, self-funded, and level-funded health plans actually differ in how an employer's premium dollars flow, who carries the risk, and where the savings come from?
chapters.title: Fully Insured vs. Self-Funded vs. Level-Funded: The Funding Architecture
chapters.subtitle: Premium mechanics, claims funds, fixed admin costs, surplus refunds, and why double-digit renewals push small and mid-size employers off fully insured plans
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners across benefits brokerages, stop-loss carriers and healthcare finance channels converge on one architecture map: fully insured is guaranteed cost where the carrier keeps every unspent claims dollar, self-funded is pay-as-you-go with stop-loss backstops, and level-funded is the hybrid that bills a fixed monthly amount split into admin, stop-loss and a claims fund with surplus refunds. Street numbers include 60-70% of self-funded spend landing in claims, carriers loading level-funded rates roughly 25% above expected cost, surplus splits of 50-80%, and level-funded penetration jumping from 10% to 45% of lives in 50-500 employee groups. Disagreements center on where the size cutoffs sit (25, 30, 45, 100 lives), whether carriers quietly keep level-funded surpluses, and how hard medical underwriting, lasers and renewal spikes bite after a bad claims year.

key_metrics.metric: Level-Funded Share of Lives in 50-500 Employee Groups
key_metrics.value: About 10% ten years ago to 45% today
key_metrics.context: Dr. Eric Bricker describes level funding as having more than quadrupled in the mid-market, concentrated in the Midwest and South.

key_metrics.context: Share of an unused claims fund returned as cash or lower next-year rates, depending on the specific contract.

key_metrics.metric: Self-Funded Plan Spend Going to Claims
key_metrics.context: Spencer Smith's estimate for small to midsize self-funded employers; fixed costs drop to roughly 25% to 30% of budget.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner starts from the same baseline: fully insured is a guaranteed-cost product where the carrier owns the upside. Spencer Smith of Self-Funded frames it as prepaid cost, with the carrier projecting claims, calculating administrative charges, collecting taxes and baking its desired profit margin into one premium, so the employer spends that full amount no matter what happens in the claims bucket unless enrollment drops significantly [VPeObJ32l7M @ 00:00:49]. Matt Roy of Blue Ocean Benefits & Consulting puts it bluntly: you pay a premium, 100% of it goes to the carrier, and the carrier keeps it regardless of what the claims are [D23XjGg7o_g @ 00:00:58]. Tyler Dutchover runs the street version of that math: a business paying $300,000 in premium whose young workforce only burns $100,000 of care watches the carrier keep every penny of the $200,000 difference, gets no refund or thank-you, and then gets higher rates the next year [ExcUj28jzzc @ 00:01:16]. Brian Calvert of Health Insurance Doesn't Have to Suck sums up the trade as maximum predictability, maximum cost, noting the model works as a starting point under 50 employees but starts leaving money on the table as a group gets larger and more stable [y9n2wYoPMYw @ 00:01:46].

The second point of consensus is what level funding actually is under the hood. Dr. Eric Bricker of AHealthcareZ calls it a crossbreed: a fixed monthly premium to the carrier, like fully insured, that funds claims plus stop-loss insurance plus an administrative fee plus the PBM, with a refund or credit possible if claims come in low and stop-loss covering the year if claims run hot [wshiRRBh4Gs @ 00:00:20]. Tyler Dutchover and Brian Calvert describe the identical three-bucket split, admin fee, stop-loss premium and a claims fund that pays everyday doctor visits and prescriptions, with leftover money coming back as a refund or credit [ExcUj28jzzc @ 00:02:16] [y9n2wYoPMYw @ 00:04:06]. The practitioners also agree that self-funding is less of a cliff than its name suggests. Matt Roy repeats a line from an old rep that a self-funded plan is really a fully reinsured self-funded plan, because individual and aggregate stop-loss cap exposure, and only very big companies take 100% of the risk, something Roy says you will not see under a thousand lives [D23XjGg7o_g @ 00:00:30]. That shared stop-loss floor is why most speakers treat the three models as points on one dial, trading predictability against how much unspent claims money the employer keeps.

Speakers also line up on who belongs in which model, and the real dividing line is claims risk. Bricker says the number one driver of claims is age, so young groups sitting in fully insured should generally go level funded, while older, high-claims groups are left holding the bag; brokers now describe the fully insured market as essentially a high-risk pool, and Bricker warns that if you don't know who the sucker at the poker table is, it's probably you [wshiRRBh4Gs @ 00:08:05]. Tyler Dutchover calls the same dynamic a death spiral, healthy groups exit, the community pool gets sicker, rates rise again, and points to Connecticut as a place where it has already happened [m5BLhBDIZZ4 @ 00:07:13]. Olivia of Allstate Benefits adds that four out of five years groups perform better than expected, so the self-funded or level-funded employer reaps that margin instead of the fully insured carrier, which also hands the group very little data on providers, claims spend or drug usage [hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:05:35]. Jennifer Shafer of JS Benefits Group turns that into the baseline prerequisite: the question is not whether level funding is cheaper but whether it fits the group's demographics, claims history and risk profile [qE34fv4L2qU @ 00:01:13].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The level-funded rate is built, not guessed, and the speakers expose the formula. Matt Roy says the carrier calculates what it needs for admin, individual stop-loss, aggregate stop-loss and claims, then usually charges about 25% more than it expects the plan to cost and hands over one flat number that looks like a fully insured premium, with some or all of the overage split back at year end depending on the contract [D23XjGg7o_g @ 00:05:15]. Olivia of Allstate Benefits mirrors that figure from the stop-loss side: the aggregate is set around 125% of expected claims, spread over 12 months, and if a major claim hits in January before the fund is built, Allstate advances the money and recoups it as the fund fills [hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:16:41]. Tyler Dutchover's 40-employee model runs $30,000 a month, $6,000 to admin, $8,000 to stop-loss and $16,000 to the claims fund, totaling $192,000 a year; a healthy year using $92,000 leaves $100,000, of which the employer gets 50 to 80% back [ExcUj28jzzc @ 00:03:06]. In the Mediocre Corp case, a $500,000 fully insured quote becomes a $470,000 level-funded cap at $39,000 monthly, with $120,000 for admin and stop-loss and $350,000 in claims reserve that technically belongs to the company [m5BLhBDIZZ4 @ 00:02:13].

Stop-loss is the engine every architecture except fully insured runs on, and the attachment points decide how much risk the employer actually carries. Matt Roy's worked example: with a $30,000 individual stop-loss, a $100,000 hospital claim costs the employer the first $30,000 and the carrier the next $70,000, and even a $2 million claim only costs the employer $30,000 [D23XjGg7o_g @ 00:02:49]. Aggregate stop-loss is the second layer, adding up every claim below the individual cap, so a $5,000, a $10,000 and a $50,000 claim capped at 30 total $45,000 toward the aggregate; Roy notes a group can hit the aggregate with nobody hitting the individual layer, though it rarely happens [D23XjGg7o_g @ 00:04:09]. Olivia says the specific deductible is the employer's choice, as low as 10 or 20 thousand or as high as 40, 50 or 100 thousand, with the aggregate deductible capping total group spend [hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:07:12]. Marc Combs of Self Insured Reporting frames the same two risks in plain terms: specific risk is one employee hit by a bus with a half-million-dollar claim, reinsured at 50,000 up to 500,000 depending on size, and aggregate risk is everybody getting the bird flu at five grand apiece [5PxkF9WUCd0 @ 00:07:44].

The vendor stack is where level-funded and self-funded split hardest. Bricker says level-funded buyers are stuck with the carrier's PBM, Cigna means Express Scripts, Aetna means CVS Caremark, United means OptumRx, and the carrier's stop-loss, while a self-funded group can carve out the PBM or buy stop-loss from Berkeley or Tokio Marine [wshiRRBh4Gs @ 00:01:18]. Olivia says Allstate runs bundled level-funded and traditional self-funded deals through Allied Benefits as TPA on about 95% of groups, with Meritain in some regions, quotes level-funded as three line items, admin, stop-loss premium and claims funding, and will sell standalone stop-loss to very large groups that want their own TPA and PBM [hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:11:13]. Getting a level-funded quote at all means underwriting: Warp reports some carriers require every employee to complete an Individual Medical Questionnaire taking three to five minutes each, non-IMQ options leave rates a shot in the dark, and brokers dodge level funding because chasing every IMQ is more work for the same job [XHSDGFk6y94 @ 00:02:08]. Marc Combs pushes the last lever: commissions run around 5% of the fully insured dollar, and after about 15 years teaching this Combs argues brokers should be fee-based, paid by the hour like accountants and attorneys for known, visible work [5PxkF9WUCd0 @ 00:05:13].

callout.title: Moves the Renewal Broker Will Not Volunteer
callout.body: These are the leverage plays the practitioners use to stop the carrier from quietly pocketing a healthy group's claims margin and to move up the funding ladder on their own terms.
items: Run the loss-ratio math on your own renewal: a 120-employee Dallas group at a 60% loss ratio got a flat renewal and no refund, leaving roughly $560,000 of about $1.4 million in premium with the carrier [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — wshiRRBh4Gs @ 00:03:45]

Use a level-funded year as a data harvest: Allstate will look at traditional self-funding for groups under 100 lives when they arrive with level-funded claims data proving they run well [Maximize Asset Protection — hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:09:05]
Convert broker pay from roughly 5% commission to a fee you can see, paid like an accountant or attorney for known work [Self Insured Reporting — 5PxkF9WUCd0 @ 00:05:13]

Hunt a broker willing to grind the IMQ paperwork: Warp says typical brokers skip level funding because of the extra work, while Warp has produced quotes showing 60% plus savings [Warp — XHSDGFk6y94 @ 00:00:48]

sop_steps.title: Strip the premium dollar
sop_steps.action: Break the current fully insured renewal into premium tax, commission, carrier retention and claims before shopping alternatives.
sop_steps.detail: Marc Combs maps a fully insured dollar at about 2 cents premium tax, about 5 cents commission, a carrier retention slice and 70 to 75 cents in medical and pharmacy claims, and says self-insuring shrinks tax and commission while cutting into carrier profit [Self Insured Reporting — 5PxkF9WUCd0 @ 00:01:28]. Brian Calvert pegs carrier overhead, margin and profit at 15 to 20 cents of every fully insured dollar [Health Insurance Doesn't Have to Suck — y9n2wYoPMYw @ 00:03:04].

sop_steps.title: Size-match the architecture
sop_steps.action: Place the group on the headcount ladder before requesting any level-funded or self-funded quote.
sop_steps.detail: Calvert's ladder: under 10 employees fully insured, 10 or 15 to 100 the level-funded sweet spot, over 100 self-funded [Health Insurance Doesn't Have to Suck — y9n2wYoPMYw @ 00:06:49]. Allstate sends traditional self-funded deals to underwriting at 100 lives, going smaller only with level-funded claims data in hand [Maximize Asset Protection — hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:08:46].

sop_steps.title: Run the underwriting sprint
sop_steps.action: Push every enrolling employee through the medical questionnaire fast and screen the census for high-cost conditions.
sop_steps.detail: Warp clocks the IMQ at three to five minutes per employee, with everyone required to finish it on IMQ carriers [Warp — XHSDGFk6y94 @ 00:02:08]. Tyler Dutchover warns underwriters can decline an older group with conditions like rheumatoid arthritis or hemophilia, or set the claims reserve so high the plan costs more than fully insured [Tyler Dutchover — m5BLhBDIZZ4 @ 00:05:13].

sop_steps.title: Lock stop-loss terms and refund mechanics
sop_steps.action: Set the specific deductible, confirm the aggregate corridor, and read the surplus split and renewal provisions before signing.
sop_steps.detail: Olivia sets the specific deductible anywhere from 10 or 20 thousand up to 100 thousand, with the aggregate around 125% of expected claims as the hard ceiling [Maximize Asset Protection — hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:07:43]. Jennifer Shafer insists on knowing the contract, stop-loss coverage, renewal provisions and financial exposure, and says never renew automatically [JS Benefits Group — UhT4cGnMRpY @ 00:01:12].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over where level funding sits on the ladder. Dr. Eric Bricker treats it as a halfway house the carrier still milks: he has run self-funded groups as small as 45 employees and says self-funding 120-employee groups is fairly common in the South and Midwest [wshiRRBh4Gs @ 00:04:30]. Olivia of Allstate Benefits pitches level funding as the stepping stone, with traditional self-funded only going to her underwriters at 100 lives unless a smaller group arrives with clean claims data from a prior level-funded year [hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:08:46]. Brian Calvert draws the cleanest map: under 10 employees start fully insured, 10 or 15 to 100 is the level-funded sweet spot, and past 100 self-funding becomes worth exploring once claims history is stable [y9n2wYoPMYw @ 00:07:03]. Floors drift by seller. Matt Roy says Cigna, Aetna and UnitedHealthcare write level-funded contracts down to 25 lives depending on state, while noting nobody under 1,000 lives carries 100 percent of the risk alone [D23XjGg7o_g @ 00:03:05]. Jennifer Shafer flags roughly 30 employees as the evaluation trigger, and David at Imago Dei opens the conversation at 10. Across the four, the floor moves with whoever is selling, and Olivia's rule holds: prior level-funded claims data is what earns a sub-100 group a self-funded look.

Nobody agrees on the size of the prize. Warp says its own level-funded quotes have produced 60 percent plus cost savings [XHSDGFk6y94 @ 00:00:48], while Bricker cites a Milliman study pegging level-funded savings at about 6 to 12 percent of overall cost [wshiRRBh4Gs @ 00:06:23]. Tyler Dutchover's Mediocre Corp model sits at the low end: a $500,000 fully insured quote against a $470,000 level-funded cap, paid at $39,000 a month [m5BLhBDIZZ4 @ 00:02:13]. Olivia flatly refuses to throw out a number, saying it depends on coverage, network and what the group wants, and frames the move as a strategy play more than a dollar play [hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:13:08]. The surplus split is just as contested. Dutchover's other walkthrough says the carrier hands back anywhere from 50 to 80 percent of unused claims money depending on contract, as cash or lower rates. Matt Roy says the carrier pads its flat price about 25 percent above expected cost and then returns some or all of the leftover. Bricker's live Dallas case got neither: a 60 percent loss ratio, no credit, no refund, flat renewal. Read every contract for the split, because three practitioners report three different refund realities on the same product.

Practitioners even disagree on what self-funded means. PeopleKeep defines it as the employer assuming total financial risk and forgoing stop-loss entirely, citing KFF data that 20 percent of covered workers at small organizations sat in self-insured plans in 2024 [o5eOH2AXJAs @ 00:01:46]. Matt Roy says the opposite: no medical group plan is truly self-funded because it is always reinsured, a fully reinsured self-funded plan in his old rep's words [D23XjGg7o_g @ 00:00:30], and Calvert says self-funded plans almost always carry stop-loss. The control argument splits too. Bricker warns level funding locks you into the carrier's stop-loss and PBM, so Cigna means Express Scripts, Aetna means CVS Caremark and United means OptumRx, while true self-funding lets you shop stop-loss with Berkeley or Tokio Marine and carve out pharmacy [wshiRRBh4Gs @ 00:01:18]. Olivia's Allstate sells standalone stop-loss to groups that want their own TPA and PBM, but she says that appetite rarely shows up below a couple hundred to thousands of lives [hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:12:38]. PeopleKeep pushes a fourth exit altogether, a standalone HRA with a fixed monthly allowance that rolls over and reimburses more than 200 expense types, and Imago Dei says the right answer for some employers is a different strategy altogether, such as direct primary care.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap is assuming a good year pays you. Bricker's Dallas broker had a 120-employee, 240-member group run a 60 percent loss ratio on roughly $1.4 million in premium at about $15,000 per subscriber; the carrier refused any credit or refund and simply held the renewal flat, pocketing about $560,000 that a self-funded group would have largely kept [wshiRRBh4Gs @ 00:04:09]. The bad year is worse. Dutchover's Mediocre Corp blows through its $350,000 claims reserve to $430,000, stop-loss covers the $80,000 overage, and total spend stays capped at $470,000, but the next renewal lands with a significant increase and possibly a laser that pushes one sick employee's specific stop-loss attachment to $200,000 [m5BLhBDIZZ4 @ 00:06:25]. Warp confirms that a significant medical claims year will hit level-funded renewal rates hard and that the group must actively manage its stop-loss [XHSDGFk6y94 @ 00:01:04]. Dutchover's escape hatch costs money: the fully insured community pool must take the group back with no health questions, but at 10 percent or more above the old rate, so $500,000 becomes roughly $550,000 [m5BLhBDIZZ4 @ 00:06:50]. Price that fallback before signing year one, since neither the good-year refund nor the bad-year renewal is locked in.

The second wall is underwriting friction before you ever see savings. Warp reports some carriers require every employee to complete an Individual Medical Questionnaire that takes three to five minutes each, a grind across hundreds of employees, while non-IMQ quotes leave rates a shot in the dark; level funding is also unavailable in some states [XHSDGFk6y94 @ 00:02:08]. Warp says that workload is exactly why many brokers never raise the option. Dutchover adds that an older workforce with a few chronic cases such as rheumatoid arthritis or hemophilia can get a group declined outright, or quoted with a claims reserve so high that level funding costs more than staying fully insured [m5BLhBDIZZ4 @ 00:05:25]. On traditional self-funded, the danger is liquidity. Olivia warns that a couple of massive claims early in the year can force the employer to pay the full aggregate amount within a couple of months, which is why the route skews to larger groups with cash on hand [hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:17:30]. Level funding softens that, since Allstate advances money when the claims fund runs short in month one and recoups it over later deposits. Matt Roy adds a back-end trap: when a self-funded contract ends, somebody still has to pay the claims that arrive afterward [D23XjGg7o_g @ 00:06:56].

The structural failure is the fully insured death spiral. Bricker says brokers now describe the fully insured market as essentially a high-risk pool, with one broker facing an 80 percent renewal and another relieved to take 30 percent, because young, low-claim groups keep leaving for level funding [wshiRRBh4Gs @ 00:08:30]. Dutchover reports the same spiral and says it has already played out in Connecticut [m5BLhBDIZZ4 @ 00:07:25]. If you are fully insured and cannot spot the sucker at the table, Bricker's line is that it is probably you. The overpay is real on the ground: Mario of Maximize Asset Protection paid UnitedHealthcare about $1,200 a month for a healthy family of four that he says never used the plan once, a $64,000 lesson he blames on buying out of fear instead of knowledge [hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:20:45]. Marc Combs of Self Insured Reporting closes the loop: no one pays your claims but you. A fully insured group that pays $1 million in premium and runs $2 million in claims gets that money clawed back at renewal, and he calls post-ACA loss-ratio optics a shell game where a 75-cent payout can hide money flowing back to the carrier [5PxkF9WUCd0 @ 00:09:30].

callout.title: Four Kill Switches Before Moving a Group Off Fully Insured
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a loss, a laser, or a cash squeeze a practitioner described firsthand. Clear all four before signing a level-funded or self-funded contract.
items: Get the surplus-split and renewal language in writing before signing, because a 120-employee group with a 60 percent loss ratio still got no credit, no refund, and a flat renewal [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — wshiRRBh4Gs @ 00:04:09].

Model the year-two downside: a renewal laser that pushes one employee's specific attachment to $200,000, plus the 10 percent or higher fully insured fallback rate [Tyler Dutchover — m5BLhBDIZZ4 @ 00:06:25].
On traditional self-funded, prove the business can write a check for the full aggregate amount within a couple of months if big claims hit early [Maximize Asset Protection — hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:17:42].

Never pick a level-funded plan just because the initial quote looks cheaper; check demographics, claims history, expected utilization, and the stop-loss protection first [JS Benefits Group — qE34fv4L2qU @ 00:00:54].

chapters.pull_quote: If you're a fully insured group and you don't know who the sucker is, it's probably you. - AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained (wshiRRBh4Gs @ 00:08:05).
action_checklist: Pull every scrap of claims data you can before renewal, because fully insured carriers are very stingy with the data they release to groups [Maximize Asset Protection — hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:09:36].
Compare fully insured, level-funded, and self-funded quotes side by side before renewal and do not automatically renew [JS Benefits Group — UhT4cGnMRpY @ 00:01:47].

Map headcount to structure: under 10 employees fully insured, 10 or 15 to 100 level funded, more than 100 self-funded with stable claims history [Health Insurance Doesn't Have to Suck — y9n2wYoPMYw @ 00:07:03].

Set the specific deductible per member, anywhere from 10,000 or 20,000 up to 100,000, and confirm the aggregate sits near 125 percent of expected claims [Maximize Asset Protection — hqPZ5l67B4A @ 00:07:43].
Budget the IMQ workload of three to five minutes per employee and demand a broker who will drive completion fast instead of skipping level funding [Warp — XHSDGFk6y94 @ 00:02:08].
Convert broker compensation to a fee-based arrangement so you know exactly what work you are paying for once you self-insure [Self Insured Reporting — 5PxkF9WUCd0 @ 00:05:13].

chapters.question_prompt: How does a broker or employer prepare, quote, and defend a level-funded case at renewal, and which plan redesign levers (direct primary care, cost navigation) actually cut spend?
chapters.title: The Level-Funding Playbook: Quoting, Renewals, and Plan Redesign
chapters.subtitle: First-case preparation, broker step-by-step questions, long-term fully insured vs. level-funded planning, common pitfalls, renewal review checklists, small-business benefit options, direct primary care, and exposing who profits from rising premiums
chapters.executive_summary: Level-funding operators from Security Health Plan, American Trust Administrators, BeneSmart and Benefit Experts converge on one model: fixed monthly payments split across administration, stop-loss and a pre-funded claims account the employer owns, with unused dollars refunded after run-out. They agree it fits healthy, stable groups that can commit to a full 12-month contract and want the upside a fully insured carrier keeps. Street mechanics are concrete: IHQs at 5 to 10 minutes per employee, quarterly wage filings, census with SIC and zip, Milliman Curve pharmacy underwriting, SHP specific stop-loss of $10,000 to $20,000 with 125% aggregate, and a 66% refund rate. Plan redesign levers include regional networks or RBP at $9 versus $25 access fees and DPC diverting about $40 PMPM. Practitioners split on surplus splits, IHQ thresholds and which carriers quote the smallest groups.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator who covered the mechanics describes level funding the same way: a self-funded plan dressed in fully insured clothing. Security Health Plan's Garrett Johnson and Erin Long frame it as "a hybrid of a traditional fully insured plan and a self-insured plan," built from three monthly cost layers (administration, specific and aggregate stop-loss, and maximum claims pre-funding) with unused claim dollars refunded after run-out [8FR_2qIAL34 @ 00:02:19]. American Trust Administrators lays out the identical skeleton: a claims account, an admin bucket covering TPA, broker, PPO access and RBP repricer, and stop-loss, paid in level monthly installments with a true-up at year end, where "the claims account is the employer's money" [QBs9tuVEIhw @ 00:04:16]. BeneSmart's Rich strips it down further, calling it "simply a self-funded plan that is fully funded," assembled from four parts (TPA, network, PBM and stop-loss) and stressing that "your costs will not vary throughout the year" [UOjbo9Dprhw @ 00:08:13]. Benefit Experts pitches the same trade to small-business owners: steady monthly costs with a refund available if claims run low, a refund they tag as "Possible, not promised" [-KHMJD6TdmM @ 00:00:37]. The shared operating premise is ownership. The employer funds its own claims bucket, keeps what it does not spend, and caps the downside with stop-loss instead of renting coverage from a carrier that keeps every surplus dollar.

The practitioners agree just as hard on who should stay out of level funding. Tom Stein, CEO of the family-owned ATA, says "level funding is not for groups that have above average claims experiences," and he flags high ER utilizers, owners selling within one to two years, and seasonal or layoff-prone workforces as bad bets, because "level funding is a long-term solution" [dgpkKOJBv_s @ 00:01:22]. Security Health Plan's sweet spot matches: healthy ACA, grandfathered or transitional groups, or smaller large groups using level funding as a stepping stone to full self-funding, typically 10 to 100 enrolled employees excluding family members [8FR_2qIAL34 @ 00:03:58]. ATA's broker-question video names the only two legitimate disqualifiers as too many claims or an inability to commit to a 12-month contract [ise8qdroICE @ 00:01:42]. The farm-analogy episode adds the time-horizon test: "you need to know that you're going to be in business for the next 12 months before level funding, which is a self-funded program, starts to make sense" [8scqEaAolto @ 00:02:16]. The consensus filter is three questions asked before any quote gets pulled: is the group healthy, will it be around and intact for at least a full contract year, and does the owner actually want to keep the upside rather than hand it to a carrier.

The renewal is the trigger every speaker builds around. ATA aims its pitch at employers with 5 to 100 employees staring at a 20% fully insured increase, opening with one question, "Have we looked at level funded?", and noting the product has "been around for three and a half decades" while many brokers skip it "simply because it's a lot more work for them" [ise8qdroICE @ 00:00:59]. BeneSmart reports fully insured carriers raising rates 10 to 15% and says 45% of employers in the 5 to 200 life space have already left for level funded or self-funded plans [UOjbo9Dprhw @ 00:05:10]. Jennifer Shafer of JS Benefits Group refuses to treat the carrier's number as final: "we don't believe your employee benefit strategy should simply be about accepting the renewal your insurance carrier gives you," and she reviews plan design, claims, population and funding options instead [6P2sMVFtCtk @ 00:00:37]. ATA's verdict on the fully insured side is blunt: "All of the upside is retained by the insurance provider, the carrier" [8scqEaAolto @ 00:01:44]. The operator takeaway is consistent across the room. A big renewal is the opening to re-market into level funding, and ATA's instruction for a broker who will not run those numbers is to go find another broker.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Quoting starts with paperwork, and every underwriter on the panel wants the same packet. ATA's first-case checklist is the quarterly wage and tax report, enrollment forms and IHQs collected under a boss-set Friday deadline, plus census, SIC code and zip code, all routed through a general agent out to carriers, TPAs, pricers and MGUs [E2z3UzEl2Ds @ 00:01:14]. ATA's broker video budgets IHQs at "5 to 10 minutes from each one of your employees" and uses the quarterly wage filing to validate who actually belongs on the plan [ise8qdroICE @ 00:02:28]. Security Health Plan underwrites with Milliman's Curve pharmacy tool, which requires a full member census, layers on medical applications that Erin Long admits are a "tough pill to swallow," and pulls 24 months of claims experience where it exists [8FR_2qIAL34 @ 00:14:19]. BeneSmart's Rich works the larger end of the market: he submits the current carrier invoice, renewals, MLRs and high-cost claimant reports, and reserves IHQs for groups under 25 [UOjbo9Dprhw @ 00:16:20]. ATA's rule for the whole process is that "level funding rewards honesty and it punishes shortcuts," and that clean submissions for underwriting produce better plans and better renewals long term, so shaded or incomplete IHQs come back to bite the broker at the very first renewal.

Pricing turns on stop-loss and on how the surplus gets split. Security Health Plan quotes specific stop-loss between $10,000 and $20,000 and aggregate at 120 to 125%; its own specific limit steps by contract count, with $10,000 for 10 to 25 contracts, $15,000 for 26 to 50, and $20,000 for 51 to 100, while aggregate stays fixed at 125 [8FR_2qIAL34 @ 00:19:02]. SHP's worked refund example pre-funds $120,000 of claims, spends $95,000, and returns $15,000 to $25,000 depending on a 60 to 100% refund rate; its current rate is 66% of unused claim dollars after run-out. ATA pushes brokers to ask "What's my surplus?" and to target 100% retention over time, stair-stepping toward it if needed [ise8qdroICE @ 00:05:09]. ATA's time-horizon matrix ties the split to tenure: a 50% surplus split, which it calls sharecropping, may fit a 1-year to 18-month horizon, while 2 to 3-plus years calls for 100% [8scqEaAolto @ 00:04:50]. On the carrier side, BeneSmart lists minimums of Cigna 25, UHC 5 and BCBS/Anthem 10, says Aetna will level fund down to two lives in certain markets, counts roughly 15 unbundled TPA partners, and treats admin and stop-loss fees as negotiable every year [UOjbo9Dprhw @ 00:12:35].

Plan redesign is where the renewal savings get manufactured. Security Health Plan runs level funding on a fixed SPD with 12 preset designs per network, while true self-funded designs flex within ERISA and ACA rules [8FR_2qIAL34 @ 00:18:24]. ATA's network play is to question whether a group even needs a national network like Cigna or Aetna: a tight regional network or RBP tends to carry "better discounts" and lower access fees, $9 a month against $25, and a knee surgery at $22,500 locally versus $25,000 nationally adds up to tens of thousands of dollars a year on a 50-life group, at the cost of fewer hospitals [ise8qdroICE @ 00:04:18]. BeneSmart stacks steerage, direct contracts, RBP and DPC on top of the funding change, and uses the savings to push zero or disappearing deductibles [UOjbo9Dprhw @ 00:06:35]. Milliman actuary Fritz Busch, on Hint Health's panel, puts a number on the DPC lever: against an $85 fee, diverted claims are worth about $40 PMPM and avoided services about $25, covering roughly 80% of the fee before quality and health-improvement value are counted, and he calls DPC a slam dunk for high-cost groups [5ztwBEIpJjs @ 00:19:47]. Busch also tells operators not to build a pro forma straight off those study figures, so the DPC math belongs in the pitch as directional support.

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Surplus splits draw the sharpest line between carrier and TPA playbooks. Security Health Plan frames the refund as a dial: on $120,000 pre-funded with $95,000 used, the $25,000 left over returns $15,000 to $25,000 at a 60 to 100 percent refund rate, and SHP itself currently pays back 66 percent of unused claim dollars at the end of the run-out period [8FR_2qIAL34 @ 00:08:16] [8FR_2qIAL34 @ 00:15:46]. American Trust Administrators treats anything short of full retention as a negotiating target. Their broker script tells employers they are entitled to their claims data and should aim for 100 percent surplus retention over time, with stair-stepping toward that number acceptable [ise8qdroICE @ 00:05:09]. The same firm's farm analogy brands a 50 percent split as sharecropping, since unused crop should stay in your own granary, yet it concedes that a 50 percent surplus can fit an owner with a one-year to 18-month horizon, while two to three years or more should command the full 100 percent [8scqEaAolto @ 00:04:12]. The operator read is blunt: the refund percentage is a contract term to match against how long the owner expects to stay in business, and it belongs on the table at every quote and every renewal rather than accepted as a fixed feature of the product.

Practitioners split on how heavy the underwriting file should be. American Trust Administrators makes individual health questionnaires non-negotiable, budgeting five to ten minutes per employee and pairing them with quarterly wage and tax filings that validate who actually belongs on the plan [ise8qdroICE @ 00:02:28]. Their pitfalls video adds that IHQs are how the plan gets priced to the reality of that group. Rich at BeneSmart runs a lighter file built on the carrier invoice, renewals, MLRs and high-cost claimant reports, reserving IHQs for groups under 25 [UOjbo9Dprhw @ 00:16:20]. Security Health Plan sits between the two: it pulls Milliman curve pharmacy data off a full member census, uses 24 months of claims experience where it exists, and still requires medical applications that the team admits are a tough pill to swallow [8FR_2qIAL34 @ 00:14:19]. Carrier floors diverge as well. Rich lists Cigna at 25, UHC at 5 and BCBS or Anthem at 10, and says Aetna will level fund all the way down to two in certain markets, while SHP writes 10 to 100 enrolled employees, excluding family members [UOjbo9Dprhw @ 00:12:35]. The practical consequence: the same census can be quotable at one carrier and dead at another, which is why ATA routes submissions through a GA to carriers, TPAs, pricers and MGUs.

The ladder from fully insured to self-funded is contested too. Security Health Plan pitches level funding to healthy ACA, grandfathered or transitional groups, and to smaller large groups as a stepping stone to self-funding [8FR_2qIAL34 @ 00:03:58]. American Trust Administrators sizes level funding at 5 to 250 lives and self-funding at 125 lives and up depending on CFO sophistication, flags a $500,000 cash call on a 250-life self-funded group, and says flatly not to self-fund below 100 lives [QBs9tuVEIhw @ 00:08:36]. Other operators never lead with level funding at all. Benefit Experts lays four options side by side: a small group plan where the business sets its premium share, a level-funded plan for relatively healthy teams whose refund is possible, not promised, an HRA with a fixed monthly allowance, and payroll-deducted voluntary benefits that can cost the company nothing [-KHMJD6TdmM @ 00:00:37]. Gusto's self-serve flow recommends small-group, level-funded and health-allowance plans by location and headcount and claims small group prices are set by law and don't vary by broker, while on the level-funded side ATA warns that brokers dodge the product because it is more work and tells owners to find another broker if theirs refuses to look [z_Qpt9fQLWg @ 00:01:03]. Benefit Experts starts every engagement with budget and people before showing a single option.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap is leaving early. American Trust Administrators states it is not a good idea to leave a level-funded plan early, because stop-loss will not honor a broken contract [TKRoJd6Glxw @ 00:01:20]. Tom Stein frames it as a 12-month contract that no group should terminate off of, and screens out owners planning to sell within one to two years plus seasonal or layoff-prone workforces [dgpkKOJBv_s @ 00:03:35]. ATA's long-term comparison sets the bar plainly: you need to know you will be in business for the next 12 months before level funding starts to make sense [8scqEaAolto @ 00:02:16]. Runout is the second shock. Contracts are expressed as 12/18 or 12/24, and under a 12/24 a group that runs well in year one still has that money sitting in accounts for an additional 12 months; ATA's example is a $115,000 surplus that does not reach the employer until a year later [TKRoJd6Glxw @ 00:05:38]. The same video notes savings sit outside the benefit trust and can fund something like a work truck, which makes the delay real money an owner is waiting on. Show the runout math before signature or the owner will expect a refund check at month thirteen.

Late claims and admin drag are the operational bottlenecks. ATA reports an MRI billed four years after the fact that turned into a negotiation, and says that conversation happens a couple of times a year across its book of business [TKRoJd6Glxw @ 00:02:39]. The same firm lists the paperwork load that comes with the plan: 1095-Bs, PCORI and an annual 5500. Speed is the other trap. ATA opens its first-case walkthrough by admitting this is not as fast as fully insured and warns brokers not to oversell speed to the client [E2z3UzEl2Ds @ 00:04:11]. Rich at BeneSmart wants enrollment done 30 days before the start date and reports seeing it squeezed to seven days, then describes the post-launch mess: providers confused by the logo on the new ID card, fixable through education [UOjbo9Dprhw @ 00:10:38]. Design freedom is also narrower: Security Health Plan's level-funded groups choose from 12 preset designs per network under a fixed SPD, while self-funded employers get flexible designs within ERISA and ACA rules [8FR_2qIAL34 @ 00:18:24]. Budget the calendar for paperwork, provider education and a 30-day enrollment window before quoting an effective date. ATA's rule for every surprise on the case is to share the bad news early.

Underwriting dishonesty and bad-risk groups blow up the economics fastest. Tom Stein is direct that level funding is not for groups with above-average claims experience and flags high ER use as a disqualifier [dgpkKOJBv_s @ 00:01:22]. ATA's case-prep rule is that level funding rewards honesty and punishes shortcuts, or in harder terms, rewards the honest and punishes the liars; clean submissions produce better plans and better renewals long term [E2z3UzEl2Ds @ 00:02:31]. The vendor-side numbers need the same scrutiny. In the Hint Health panel, Milliman actuary Fritz Busch prices an $85 DPC fee against roughly $40 PMPM in diverted claims and $25 in avoided claims, about $68 in total, leaving a $17 gap that quality value closes to break-even, and explicitly warns against building a pro forma from those figures [5ztwBEIpJjs @ 00:20:18]. Dave Chase adds the broker-side check: Health Rosetta found up to 17 undisclosed revenue streams the employer didn't know about, and the fix starts with getting access to claims data, by demand letter if needed [nrL0pYx-hQo @ 00:22:04]. Clint Flanigan of Nextera separately warns about commission-paid brokers. Tom Stein's last check is behavioral: if the client doesn't know it is their money, part of the value of level funding is taken away.

callout.body: These four gates come straight from the pitfalls ATA, BeneSmart and Security Health Plan report seeing on live cases. Fail one and the case either gets priced wrong, terminates off contract, or launches into provider confusion.
items: Walk away if the group runs above-average claims, shows high ER use, or the owner plans to sell within one to two years [American Trust Administrators | Level Funding — dgpkKOJBv_s @ 00:01:22].
Do not bind until the client accepts the 12-month contract and the 12/18 or 12/24 runout that delays surplus [American Trust Administrators | Level Funding — TKRoJd6Glxw @ 00:05:52].
Hold submission until every IHQ and the quarterly wage and tax report are collected, with the boss setting a Friday deadline [American Trust Administrators | Level Funding — E2z3UzEl2Ds @ 00:01:14].

Pull the carrier invoice, renewals, MLRs and high-cost claimant reports before quoting, and collect IHQs for groups under 25 [BeneSmart - A Modern Approach to Benefits — UOjbo9Dprhw @ 00:15:03].

Price a tight regional network or RBP against the national network, using the $9 versus $25 monthly access fee and the $22,500 versus $25,000 knee surgery spread [American Trust Administrators | Level Funding — ise8qdroICE @ 00:04:03].

chapters.question_prompt: How does stop-loss insurance protect a self-funded plan, and what contract terms decide whether a catastrophic claim actually gets reimbursed?
chapters.title: Stop-Loss Insurance: Specific, Aggregate, and the Contract Traps
chapters.subtitle: Specific vs. aggregate coverage, aggregate corridors, aggregating specific deductibles, lasers, MGUs, reimbursement mechanics, filing stop-loss claims, and who pays the million-dollar claim
chapters.executive_summary: Stop-loss practitioners agree on the foundation: it is a reimbursement contract owned by the self-funded employer, split into specific coverage for catastrophic individual claims and aggregate coverage capping total plan spend. Spencer, Pete Dorne, and the Self-Funded Sketchbook put 80 to 90% of premium into the specific layer, while aggregate is cheap sleep insurance built on expected claims plus a 25% corridor that pays out for under 3% of groups. The street mechanics turn on numbers: a $600,000 laser on a $150,000 spec quietly adds $450,000 of exposure, a $50,000 ag spec trades roughly dollar for dollar against premium, and unbundled PBM and TPA reporting can hide a breached deductible entirely. The fault lines run between carrier laser leverage and ag-spec counter-moves, paying for experience refunds versus taking a premium cut, and who files claims when BUCA ASO setups never send them.

key_metrics.metric: Share of Stop-Loss Premium Going to Specific Coverage

key_metrics.metric: Large Claim Severity Growth in One Policy Year

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who walks through stop-loss starts in the same place: it is a reimbursement contract bought by the self-funded employer, not by employees, and it comes in two layers that usually get bought together. Spencer of Self-Funded frames self-funding as the employer saying it will absorb and manage the risk itself, then buying specific and aggregate coverage to mitigate and predict that risk, noting that outside true jumbo employers the vast majority purchase both together [4cndcrJWUGg @ 00:01:29]. Self Insured Reporting states flatly that stop-loss covers the employer rather than the employees, with specific protecting against any single large claimant and aggregate capping the total claims the employer pays in a period [HuaDk3XBOrc @ 00:00:39]. Andrew and Don of This STUFF is complicated call reimbursement the universal truth from which everything else flows, because claims lag of 30 to 45 days, sometimes multiple months, means a claim has to be paid, measured, and processed before anyone can be repaid [q36fieahkDs @ 00:01:33]. Pete Dorne and Spencer Smith at ParetoHealth reinforce it: the employer owns the risk and writes the check, and the carrier reimburses the dollars above the deductible after the fact, which is why advance funding gets treated as a separate enhancement rather than the default [4VhWXTCGo74 @ 00:01:24].

On where the money goes, the numbers line up across speakers. Spencer puts 80 to 85% of stop-loss premium on the specific layer because the underwriter is trying to predict the wildly unpredictable individual catastrophic claim, and notes the contracts theoretically carry an unlimited maximum, so a $20 million claim still gets picked up above the deductible [4cndcrJWUGg @ 00:03:19]. In the Self-Funded Sketchbook the figure climbs to 85 to 90% or more depending on group size and deductible, with specific described as low frequency, high severity risk: a hemophiliac joining the plan or a premature baby parked in the NICU for three or four weeks [adwLQHPv5YI @ 00:02:21]. Pete Dorne confirms 85 to 90%, and adds the reason it is getting worse: one of ParetoHealth's stop-loss carrier partners saw a 45% increase in the size and severity of large claims, million-dollar-plus, in a single policy year, with claims that ran $250,000 five years ago now landing at $500,000 or $600,000 [4VhWXTCGo74 @ 00:02:06]. Tyler Dutchover lands on the same logic in plain English: because nobody can predict a three-month NICU stay or a coronary bypass, specific is the more expensive of the two coverages [b2StkpG4yOY @ 00:02:34].

Aggregate gets the opposite treatment: cheap, predictable, and rarely triggered. Spencer calls it sleep insurance, built by taking expected claims of $1 million and adding a typical 25% buffer to set a $1.25 million attachment point, with a hit on maybe two to three percent of contracts and coverage usually capped around $1 million, though some BUCAs offer unlimited [4cndcrJWUGg @ 00:05:27]. Pete Dorne derives the attachment point the same way, prior-year net claims plus trend plus a 25% aggregate corridor that sets the maximum not-to-exceed bucket on small claims, places expected claims at roughly 80% of attachment, and puts aggregate hits at less than 3% of all self-funded groups [4VhWXTCGo74 @ 00:08:54]. Spencer's corridor episode adds the kill shot on why it is cheap: with a 25% corridor the underwriter has to mispredict by 25% before aggregate pays, which takes bad data, a mistake, a genuinely terrible claims year, or an underwriter getting too aggressive on the attachment to win the business [Dy4S9Ie5mEM @ 00:05:16]. Tyler Dutchover runs it at 125% of expected claims, sometimes slightly higher, and positions aggregate as protection from death from a million cuts across the whole workforce rather than one catastrophic claimant [b2StkpG4yOY @ 00:03:37].

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Run the math the way the practitioners do. Tyler Dutchover's model: a 150-person group expecting $1.5 million in claims sets a $75,000 specific attachment; the instant one person hits $75,001 the carrier pays 100% of the rest, so a $1 million NICU baby costs the employer $75,000 and the carrier reimburses $925,000 [b2StkpG4yOY @ 00:01:26]. The group's aggregate cap at 125% lands at $1.87 million; in a brutal year that hits $2.5 million, the carrier covers the final $630,000, and the critical interaction is that the $75,000 the employer paid on the NICU claim counts toward the aggregate limit while the $925,000 the carrier paid does not [b2StkpG4yOY @ 00:04:05]. Spencer's base case is identical in structure: a $100,000 specific deductible, a $125,000 claimant, a $25,000 reimbursement, and claims can be medical only, Rx only, or combined across the policy period [4cndcrJWUGg @ 00:02:45]. Pete Dorne adds the monthly reality underneath it: the TPA bills the employer every month, the employer funds whatever utilization came in, and those swings, the EKG effect, are the employer's to carry unless year-end claims clear the attachment point or the group bought an aggregate accommodation [4VhWXTCGo74 @ 00:07:45].

Lasers are where a clean-looking renewal hides the real bill. Spencer's illustration: everyone on the plan carries a $100,000 spec, but one known high-cost claimant gets a $250,000 laser, so the employer now owns another $150,000 of risk on that person alone, and on a $300,000 claim the carrier reimburses only $50,000 [hiWm3Y4k6SI @ 00:03:17]. Carriers do it because a predictable claimant, say someone on a $20,000-a-month drug, would breach the deductible with not enough premium in the case to stay profitable, and in extreme cases they exclude the person entirely [hiWm3Y4k6SI @ 00:05:25]. Ralph Weber of Benefit Whisperer shows the trap at renewal: premium moves from $84,000 to $89,000, a single-digit increase nobody has seen in years, but a $600,000 laser on one claimant against a $150,000 spec means a $500,000 claim leaves the employer an extra $350,000, and up to $450,000 of added exposure if it passes $600,000 [6E1eObzSNLc @ 00:01:05]. Spencer's counter-move from the ag spec episode: when a small laser sits close to the spec, like $125,000 over a $100,000 deductible, offer a $50,000 ag spec in exchange for dropping it, and the carrier will often accept [VatFfWseBbI @ 00:07:34].

The ag spec is the most aggressive premium play taught. Spencer credits Scott Campbell of AmWINS with the gift-card analogy: add a $50,000 aggregating specific deductible and the carrier most often cuts premium by $50,000, but that money can only be spent on the shared layer of claims sitting above the regular spec [VatFfWseBbI @ 00:01:42]. The bucket math: claimants run $25,000 and $10,000 over a $100,000 spec, filling $35,000; a third claimant $45,000 over contributes only the $15,000 needed to fill the $50,000 bucket, and the remaining $30,000 spills to the carrier for reimbursement, with one person able to blow through both layers alone [VatFfWseBbI @ 00:05:04]. Spencer's pitch is heads you win, tails you break even: no spec claims means $50,000 saved, a full bucket means $50,000 paid against a $50,000 premium cut, and it beats an experience refund that charges roughly 5% for a chance at 10% back [VatFfWseBbI @ 00:08:18]. Once reimbursements are flowing, Andrew and Don put carrier turnaround at 10 to 12 business days about 90% of the time after submission, stretching to 15 to 20 business days at year end when filings pile up [q36fieahkDs @ 00:04:47].

callout.title: Stop-Loss Moves the Practitioners Actually Use
callout.body: These are the specific plays that separate a group that collects every reimbursement dollar from one that eats a laser or a missed filing.
items: If a BUCA is ASO only with a third-party stop-loss carrier, assume claims are not being sent; Spencer fielded broker calls at Sun Life about a $300,000 claim the carrier had never received [Self-Funded — AM2DB13I88c @ 00:02:56].

Never accept a near-spec laser at face value: offer a $50,000 ag spec in exchange for dropping a $125,000 laser on a $100,000 spec, which carriers often accept when it is that close [Self-Funded — VatFfWseBbI @ 00:07:48].

Look for plan mirroring language in the stop-loss contract so whatever the plan document covers is covered by the contract, and lean on plan document amendments for extra protection [This STUFF is complicated — q36fieahkDs @ 00:03:37].
Compare a self-funded attachment point to a fully insured renewal delayed 12 months, the 30 to 35% hit after a bad claims year, not to today's renewal [ParetoHealth — 4VhWXTCGo74 @ 00:10:01].

sop_steps.title: Set the specific deductible and aggregate corridor
sop_steps.action: Choose the per-person corporate deductible and confirm the corridor and monthly aggregate factor before the policy period starts.
sop_steps.detail: Budget monthly somewhere between expected claims and maximum liability, using the monthly aggregate factor that flexes with headcount, and confirm whether the corridor is 25%, 20%, 15%, or a 10% level-funded corridor [Self-Funded — Dy4S9Ie5mEM @ 00:02:07].

sop_steps.title: Audit the renewal for lasers before signing
sop_steps.action: Pull the stop-loss contract and check every named laser against the standard specific deductible.
sop_steps.detail: Ralph Weber's workflow: go to whatsinyourcontract.com, pick administrative services agreement, PBM, or stop-loss from the drop-down, upload the file, enter an email, and run check my contract before you renew [Benefit Whisperer — 6E1eObzSNLc @ 00:01:28].

sop_steps.title: Assign exactly one claim filer up front
sop_steps.action: Decide whether the TPA, the broker team, or a GA files stop-loss claims, and lock it in at setup.
sop_steps.detail: Get a monthly data dump, file feed, or reporting portal access from the administrator, and pick one entity so there is no duplicate filing, no reporting disconnect, and no finger-pointing later [Self-Funded — AM2DB13I88c @ 00:04:01].

sop_steps.title: Merge medical and Rx and track every claim to payment
sop_steps.action: Make sure the carrier receives both medical and PBM claim reports, then monitor each filing through reimbursement.
sop_steps.detail: Read your reports, know when a claim is going to be filed and when it has been filed, and understand what eligibility and plan document steps the carrier needs to release the money [This STUFF is complicated — q36fieahkDs @ 00:07:39].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Every practitioner agrees specific coverage absorbs most of the premium, but the split they quote differs. Spencer of Self-Funded puts roughly 80 to 85% of stop-loss premium on the spec side because the carrier is trying to predict the wildly unpredictable individual catastrophic claim [4cndcrJWUGg @ 00:03:19]. Pete Dorne of ParetoHealth answers 85 to 90% when asked the same question on the ParetoHealth channel, confirming spec is where the real dollars sit [4VhWXTCGo74 @ 00:01:52]. The corridor is where playbooks diverge most. Spencer calls a 25% buffer the most common self-funded corridor, yet reports 20% and 15% corridors in the market and 10% corridors on level funded contracts, which means the underwriter only has to miss by that smaller margin before aggregate pays [Dy4S9Ie5mEM @ 00:04:18]. Tyler Dutchover models the aggregate attachment at 125% of expected claims, sometimes slightly higher, so a 150-person group expecting 1.5 million in claims carries a 1.87 million aggregate cap, and a brutal 2.5 million year triggers a 630,000 aggregate payout [b2StkpG4yOY @ 00:03:37]. The operator takeaway: corridor width is a quoted variable, not a constant, and a tighter corridor moves the point where the cheap aggregate layer actually starts paying money back to the employer.

The cash-flow playbook splits between pure reimbursement and advance funding. Andrew Kikenbball of This STUFF is complicated calls the reimbursement structure the universal truth everything else flows from, since a claim has to be filed, adjudicated and paid, with claims lag running 30 to 45 days and sometimes multiple months [q36fieahkDs @ 00:01:33]. Lauren at Roundstone Insurance pitches the opposite experience: on a million-dollar claim against a 100,000 deductible, the employer pays the first 100,000 and does not have to pay and wait to be reimbursed, because the captive can advance it for groups that are not comfortable putting the cash out, which matters for the 50 to 300 employee sweet spot Roundstone targets [FPn0kt8qe6U @ 00:06:14]. The Benefits Group describes stop-loss the same way for level funded and self-funded plans, saying the carrier advances money into the claims account so a million-dollar claim never drains it past the 50,000 specific deductible [7-gc1zHvZbc @ 00:01:34]. PeopleKeep draws the hard line on who should skip the model: a mostly older or family-heavy workforce runs a higher claim frequency, and that employer may decide waiting for reimbursements is not worth the initial expensive claim payouts and look at alternatives to self-insured plans [87JIyLFot-o @ 00:03:19].

On lasers, two Self-Funded playbooks compete. Spencer's baseline is straight negotiation: get the carrier to pull the laser back, or if they dig in, extract some premium to offset it, and treat it as part of the game, since anyone self-funded long enough has likely had a laser imposed or at least proposed on a quote [hiWm3Y4k6SI @ 00:04:54]. Spencer's preferred counter is the ag spec swap. With a 100k spec and a 125,000 laser, the move is to throw on a 50k ag spec, take the 50,000 premium cut, and drop the laser; when the numbers are that close the stop-loss carrier often accepts, though not every underwriter will agree [VatFfWseBbI @ 00:07:34]. Spencer then attacks the experience refund directly: a carrier offering a possible 10% dividend for good claims experience will charge around 5% for it, so why pay five percent to potentially get ten back when an ag spec lowers premium without charging for the privilege [VatFfWseBbI @ 00:08:18]. Roundstone runs a different reward model, redistributing unused premium at the captive layer, and Lauren describes the best part of account management as calling a group or broker to say a percentage of premium is coming back [FPn0kt8qe6U @ 00:09:29]. One camp banks the upside as a lower premium up front; the other pays it out after the year closes.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap reported is the laser buried inside a renewal that looks friendly. Ralph Weber of Benefit Whisperer walks through a stop-loss renewal moving from 84 to 89,000, a single digit increase nobody has seen in years, with one word hidden in the contract: a 600,000 laser on one identified claimant against a 150,000 specific deductible [6E1eObzSNLc @ 00:00:29]. If that claimant runs 500,000 in eligible claims, the policy never kicks in and the employer is on the hook for an extra 350,000; once claims pass 600,000, the extra exposure reaches 450,000 [6E1eObzSNLc @ 00:01:05]. Spencer of Self-Funded explains the mechanics behind it: a claimant who is sick or projected to be sick represents known risk the carrier cannot absorb and still stay profitable, so that person gets a 250k spec while everyone else sits at 100k, leaving the employer funding another 150,000 of risk tied to a single name [hiWm3Y4k6SI @ 00:03:17]. The worst version is an outright exclusion, rare but used when someone poses millions of dollars of risk to the plan and no premium load could absorb it, at which point the carrier carves that person out of coverage entirely [hiWm3Y4k6SI @ 00:05:25]. Every laser moves dollars back onto the employer, never the other way.

Claims filing is where brokers get burned. Spencer of Self-Funded reports seeing a really big errors-and-omissions claim when someone at a broker shop dropped the ball and did not file a stop-loss claim in a timely manner, handing the carrier an opportunity to deny it [AM2DB13I88c @ 00:01:10]. The root cause is structural: with a BUCA ASO and a third-party stop-loss carrier, the ASO overwhelmingly is not sending claims to the carrier, and from Spencer's time at Sun Life, brokers would call demanding a 300,000 reimbursement only for underwriting and the claims department to respond, what claim [AM2DB13I88c @ 00:02:56]. Unbundled PBM setups add a second blind spot: a member with 10,000 in medical and 100,000 in prescription claims totals 110,000 against a 100k spec, but if only the medical reporting package reaches the carrier, nobody, including the broker, knows a stop-loss claim exists [AM2DB13I88c @ 00:05:35]. Don McCully of This STUFF is complicated puts a number on the pattern, saying that when they entered the space nine out of 10 E&O claims came from stop-loss, and pointing out that stop-loss is filed as a property and casualty product rather than accident and health [q36fieahkDs @ 00:02:25]. The exposure lands on whoever was supposed to be watching the feeds.

Contract wording and plan documents create the quieter losses. Andrew Kikenbball and Don McCully warn that the stop-loss contract does not always say what it means because reimbursement runs off the plan document, a separate contract, so operators should hunt for plan document amendments and a plan mirroring clause stating whatever is in the document is in the contract [q36fieahkDs @ 00:03:23]. PeopleKeep adds that a stop-loss carrier may have policies that refuse reimbursement for certain claims, and a misunderstanding can produce significant liability, so the document needs to be examined with the insurer or broker before the plan period begins [87JIyLFot-o @ 00:01:46]. On the aggregate side, Spencer flags that a 25% miss usually means bad data, an outright mistake, a genuinely bad claims year, or an underwriter getting way too aggressive on the attachment point to win the business [Dy4S9Ie5mEM @ 00:05:34]. Roundstone's claims team shows what unreviewed payment costs: a long hospitalization billed intermittently and then billed again for the entire stay put about a million dollars in front of them twice, and Lauren admits they would not have believed it a couple of years earlier without seeing it firsthand [FPn0kt8qe6U @ 00:22:30]. Somebody has to read the bills, not just pay them.

chapters.question_prompt: When does a medical stop-loss group captive beat traditional stop-loss or level funding for a 25–500 life employer, and how are the risk layers structured?
chapters.title: Medical Stop-Loss Captives: Pooling Risk Outside the Traditional Market
chapters.subtitle: Captive risk layers, premium-dollar transparency, individual vs. block underwriting, member-owned and industry captives (including EMS), captive vs. level-funded comparisons, and the TPA's role in the self-funded stack
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree on the basic design of a medical stop-loss captive. A self-funded employer keeps claims below a specific deductible, a member-owned pool absorbs the next layer, and an A-rated excess carrier sits on top. The goal is to stop year-two lasers, 50 percent renewal spikes, and opaque carrier pricing. The street mechanics are concrete. Captive Resources shows a $100,000 specific deductible with a $600,000 aggregate attachment. CRI reports that 60 to 65% of premium is ceded to the loss fund and $35M has been returned over 10 years. Self-Funded prices a $5 to $6 retail vendor at about $1 inside the captive. BeneSmart reports $215,000 in year-one Rx savings for one 150-life manufacturer. Operators split on three points: size floors and ceilings (16 lives to 1,000+), block versus individual underwriting, and whether retention runs at 98% or 95%.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus - Ownership, Pooling and Control
paragraphs: Every operator in this lane frames the medical stop-loss captive the same way. A self-funded employer keeps its own claims below a specific deductible, a member-owned pool absorbs the next layer, and an excess reinsurer sits on top. Captive Resources defines the group captive as an insurer owned and controlled by its insureds. The firm stresses the word CONTROL and places the captive overlay between the specific deductible and the excess layer [c_F-WNrCoqk @ 00:01:28]. Joe Perelli of Captive Resources adds that members still buy policies from A or A+ carriers. The difference is ownership, not paper quality [BQVeLgnIx8A @ 00:03:35]. On the panel hosted by Chris Martens, the captive is called an 'upside down reinsurance mechanism' that takes a layer from a carrier such as Sun Life or HCC/Berkley [M8zhsS8szwY @ 00:06:42]. Pete Thorne and Spencer Smith of Self-Funded put it more simply: a captive is 'a small insurance company' that aggregates employers who share risk. Pooling spreads that risk and reduces the 'blow on stop loss' that any single member would otherwise take [8nD9sJwgMdE @ 00:00:47]. The shared logic is that small and mid-sized firms are slow to self-fund on their own. The captive pools their buying power and gives them large-group leverage without large-group headcount.

Operators also agree on why employers move: the traditional market punishes small and mid-sized groups with opaque, volatile renewals. Captive Resources says the two traditional levers are scaling back coverage or making the company and employees pay more, and 'Neither option is great.' That matters because employees rank health insurance as their most important benefit [c_F-WNrCoqk @ 00:00:18]. Conner Strong & Buckelew names the weaknesses of stand-alone stop loss bluntly: lasers in year two and increases 'upwards of 50 percent.' Fully insured plans, by contrast, hand over no data and build in taxes and carrier profits [f50x6TivjJ4 @ 00:01:50]. Ross & Yerger answer that captive membership brings no new lasers in perpetuity, plus renewal rate caps [zzL4UNZNaFo @ 00:03:22]. Perelli explains why the stop-loss decision carries so much leverage. Stop loss is only 15 to 20% of total spend, below-deductible claims run 75 to 80%, and double-digit increases are now 'normal' [BQVeLgnIx8A @ 00:09:40]. Shopping stop loss every year therefore attacks only a fifth of the budget. The captive instead changes how the whole claims picture is managed and priced, and it rewards the employers whose claims come in better than projected.

The baseline prerequisites also line up across the field, even where headcount floors differ. Ross & Yerger target employers with 50 to 300 employees [zzL4UNZNaFo @ 00:00:03]. TheSpringGroup sets its threshold at 100+ lives because carrier data becomes accessible at that size [L4bWq8jE_JE @ 00:02:07]. Rich of BeneSmart places captives at 50+ lives but warns they do not suit groups that want hands-off arrangements [WXjUaMhMjcQ @ 00:02:09]. The most consistent filter is mindset. Thorne and Smith say employers who treat stop loss as a commodity and buy it over 12 months are 'not a fit' [8nD9sJwgMdE @ 00:05:41]. Taken together, these operators describe a specific buyer. It has enough lives to produce usable claims data and enough cash to carry a retention layer. It also has the patience to stay in a pool through the bad years rather than chase the cheapest quote at every renewal. That buyer must also be willing to engage. Data, vendor choices and renewal results all flow back to the member, so an HR team that wants to sign a form and disappear forfeits most of the structure's advantage. For every one of these operators, the captive is an operating commitment that runs across several renewal cycles, not a one-time product swap.
