sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The Omega walk-through from Captive Resources is the cleanest layer math in the field. Omega picks a $100,000 specific deductible and retains aggregate claims up to 120% of $500,000 in expected losses, which sets a $600,000 Aggregate Attachment Point. The captive then takes the next $200,000 specific, covering claims to $300,000, and the next $200,000 aggregate, from $600K to $800K. Excess reinsurance supplies unlimited specific protection plus $800,000 of aggregate protection above that [c_F-WNrCoqk @ 00:03:37]. Phil, the MedTrans captive manager, runs a comparable stack built around a $50k specific deductible. That figure drops to roughly $25k for 30 lives and rises to $200k for large groups, with 70 to 80% budgeted to claims and 10 to 15% to the captive layer [I33Yc7nNN_c @ 00:12:19]. The Self-Funded team slices the middle layer one of two ways: quota share, splitting risk 60/40 or 50/50, or their own floating layer, which takes 100% of the risk above the spec up to a cap [6st-3ujjXM4 @ 00:00:56]. Their three-layer model adds aggregate protection because executives panic at '50,000 x 200.' Every one of these operators treats the specific deductible as the dial that decides how much volatility the employer keeps and how much it pays someone else to carry.

The money flow is where the captive earns its keep. Captive Resources runs three funding mechanisms. The Member Loss Fund equals stop-loss premium minus operating costs. The Member Assessment is capped at a known percentage of that loss fund. Captive Risk Sharing spreads remaining losses across the pool [c_F-WNrCoqk @ 00:04:13]. Conner Strong & Buckelew describes the same engine as a claim stabilization pool. The carrier refunds unused premium or draws on the pool, contributions are capped, and the carrier pays if the pool runs empty [f50x6TivjJ4 @ 00:02:24]. Perelli tests fit before anyone joins with a look-back analysis that compares a member's historical large claims against its bucket. Exceeding the bucket means an assessment year, while a surplus builds an equity position [BQVeLgnIx8A @ 00:15:20]. On the Martens panel, the CRI numbers get specific. Between 60 and 65% of premium is ceded to the loss fund, and over 10 years $35M has been returned to members on a captive loss ratio of 93 to 101% [M8zhsS8szwY @ 00:55:23]. Perelli also rejects the 'overpriced' label outright. The captive layer is priced at break-even, and outperformance flows back to members as dividends and distributions instead of staying with a carrier as margin.

Pricing mechanics decide who subsidizes whom inside the pool, and by how much. Phil Helloka of Complete Captive puts the subsidy in numbers. Block-blending four groups lands the rate at $102 PEPM, so the good group pays roughly $13 PEPM over its own risk. Meanwhile, an adverse 20-life group still prices at $115 even after a 10% discount [PERxwpJ2Rnk @ 00:07:30]. Helloka's conclusion is that ultimately you want individual underwriting, because blending drags down the clean group. The increase math on the Martens panel shows the stakes. On $1M of spend, a 20% increase costs $200K fully insured, compared with $40K when the increase lands on stop loss alone [M8zhsS8szwY @ 00:57:40]. Vendor scale is the second lever. Thorne and Smith price a vendor at $5 to $6 retail for a 200-life employer and at about $1 inside the captive [8nD9sJwgMdE @ 00:01:29]. Rich of BeneSmart supplies the pharmacy proof. A 150-life manufacturer paying $35,000 a month for three drugs saved $215,000 on Rx in year one after moving to a captive [WXjUaMhMjcQ @ 00:04:53]. Rich still cautions that switching the funding model won't magically save money, but it does set the table. Once the bundled carrier layers come out, the savings compound.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is headcount. CRI's Joe Perilli sets the floor at 50 employees with a working range of 50 to 5,000, and notes TPAs rarely go below 40 lives [M8zhsS8szwY @ 00:23:05]. On the same panel, Jeff Christian pushes back that the market is moving down to 25 and that their own book already carries a 16-life member [M8zhsS8szwY @ 00:24:40]. The Paro health team on Self-Funded reframes the fight entirely: headcount is the wrong gauge, because a 1,000-life group sitting on a $500k deductible leaves too little risk premium to pool, while the same group at a $150k deductible may fit [8nD9sJwgMdE @ 00:08:07]. At the top end, Heads Up Adviser argues that groups past 250, maybe 300 lives, historically tend to outgrow the need for the captive altogether [7cqcZyKB5aw @ 00:00:21]. That puts the practical ceiling anywhere from 300 lives to 5,000 depending on who is pitching, and the floor anywhere from a live 16-life member up to the historical 100-life line the Paro team says used to govern the market. The operator read is blunt: stop arguing employee count in isolation. Size the decision on deductible level, on how much risk premium actually sits inside the captive layer, and on how much year-to-year volatility the owner can absorb.

Practitioners also split on how the middle layer is built. Captive Resources walks through the Omega example: the employer keeps the first $100,000 specific, the captive takes the next $200,000 specific up to $300,000 and the next $200,000 aggregate from $600K to $800K, funded through a member loss fund, a capped member assessment, and captive risk sharing [c_F-WNrCoqk @ 00:03:55]. Self-Funded's risk-layer breakdown describes a different engine: quota share programs split risk 60/40 or 50/50, while their own program runs a floating layer that takes 100% of the risk above the spec up to a cap [6st-3ujjXM4 @ 00:00:56]. Conner Strong & Buckelew pitches a simpler claim stabilization pool where the carrier refunds unused premium or draws on the pool, contributions are capped, and the carrier pays if the pool runs dry [f50x6TivjJ4 @ 00:02:24]. Underwriting splits too. Phil Helloka of Complete Captive shows that blending four groups into a $102 block rate charges the good group roughly $13 PEPM over its own risk [PERxwpJ2Rnk @ 00:07:30], which is why Helloka argues you ultimately want individual underwriting. Operators comparing captive offers need to ask which of these engines sits under the label, because the word captive covers a member-owned layer, a quota share, a floating layer, and a carrier-run pool.

Even the retention number is contested between partners on one stage. CRI's Joe Perilli reports 98% retention in the health captive programs [M8zhsS8szwY @ 01:00:11], while Jeff Christian puts the figure lower at 95% [M8zhsS8szwY @ 01:04:13]. Both numbers are strong, but a three-point gap on the same panel shows the headline figure moves depending on who is doing the counting. The bigger fault line is captive versus level funding. Heads Up Adviser frames captives as working much like level funding, a cash-flow protection product that 'makes me feel good at night,' and says captives may still suit groups of 200 plus [7cqcZyKB5aw @ 00:00:37]. Rich at BeneSmart draws a harder line: level funded fits 25 to 150 lives, captives fit 50 plus but not for owners who want a hands-off arrangement, and level-funded refunds are shared while the model carries spread pricing [WXjUaMhMjcQ @ 00:04:23]. Rich's own case study backs the unbundled route: a 150-life manufacturer paying $35,000 a month for three drugs saved $215,000 on Rx in year one after the move. The alternative playbook follows from that split. A group that wants cash-flow protection without unbundling anything can live inside level funding, while a group willing to pick its own TPA, PBM, and stop-loss vendor lineup is the buyer the captive crowd is actually built for.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The traditional-market trap behind most captive conversations is the laser. Conner Strong & Buckelew reports stop-loss carriers lasering claimants in year two and pushing increases upwards of 50 percent [f50x6TivjJ4 @ 00:01:50]. The Paro health team on Self-Funded says stop-loss rate caps of 50% plus are only going up, and positions the captive as the route to better reinsurance terms, no lasering, and lower caps [8nD9sJwgMdE @ 00:03:15]. Heads Up Adviser names the casualty: a group that was hit with some giant laser and forced back to fully insured may value a captive regardless of size [7cqcZyKB5aw @ 00:01:08]. Ross & Yerger frames the captive counter-offer as no new lasers in perpetuity plus renewal rate caps [zzL4UNZNaFo @ 00:03:22]. The economics check runs against the traditional side. A group that self-funds on a standalone stop-loss policy, takes a large claimant, and then gets lasered has lost the protection it bought at exactly the moment it needed it. Retreating to fully insured means walking back into a product with no data and with taxes and carrier profits built in. The practical move is to pin down lasering and rate-cap terms before renewal, because that is the specific protection every practitioner here sells the captive on.

Captives do not remove bad years; they relocate them. CRI's Chief Business Officer describes the look-back analysis: compare a member's historical large claims against its bucket, and a member that exceeds it is looking at an assessment year, while surplus becomes an equity position [BQVeLgnIx8A @ 00:15:20]. Surplus years are where the dividends and distributions come from; deficit years are where the member writes a check. Ross & Yerger puts the cycle bluntly: four of five years are good and one or two are bad [zzL4UNZNaFo @ 00:04:11]. Self-Funded's risk-layer breakdown says a captive can go as low as 20 lives, but smaller groups face claims volatility, and above about 1,000 lives the cost advantage is less obvious [6st-3ujjXM4 @ 00:02:18]. The claim sizes feeding those bad years keep climbing. On the Christopher Martens panel, the speakers cite gene therapy claims at $3.5M for hemophilia, $3M, and $2.8M [M8zhsS8szwY @ 00:38:09]. Those severities are why the Omega structure stacks unlimited specific coverage above the captive layer, and why a small member's real exposure in a bad year is the assessment rather than the headline claim. The operator read: underwrite the downside year first, because the dividend history only describes the good four out of five.

The rest of the failure list is operational. On the Martens panel, the joining warning is explicit: captives run on a common anniversary with short or long first contracts, and a group should not move mid-year while claims are accruing to the deductible [M8zhsS8szwY @ 01:06:08]. The Paro health team flags the employer who treats stop-loss as a commodity and buys over 12 months as not a fit [8nD9sJwgMdE @ 00:05:41]. That buyer misses the point the member-owned structure is built on: skin in the game, plus reserves that can lower deductibles or fund premium holidays. Phil Helloka of Complete Captive flags the trap inside block-rated programs: the good group charged over its own risk turns into a 'perpetual winner' who becomes unhappy, and ultimately you want individual underwriting [PERxwpJ2Rnk @ 00:09:48]. The economics check from the Martens panel shows why fit matters: on $1M of spend, a 20% increase costs $200K fully insured versus $40K when it lands on stop loss alone [M8zhsS8szwY @ 00:57:40]. Berkley has been fronting the same program for 13 years, and the panel's instruction is plain: do not shop the captive every year. Groups that shop the captive yearly, join mid-cycle with claims running, or accept a blended block rate without asking throw away the exact advantage they came for.

chapters.question_prompt: What do pharmacy benefit managers actually do, and how does money flow between manufacturers, PBMs, pharmacies, plans, and patients?
chapters.title: Pharmacy Benefit Managers: Following the Money
chapters.subtitle: PBM money-flow mapping, formulary tiers, rebates, spread pricing basics, PBM 'games,' industry consolidation and scrutiny, transparency claims, and the economics of owning a PBM
chapters.executive_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers sit between plan sponsors, drugmakers, wholesalers and pharmacies, and every practitioner here agrees the money is made in the gaps between contracts the buyer never sees. Three PBMs, CVS Caremark, Express Scripts and OptumRx, control roughly 80 to 85 percent of the market, run the formulary auction, and own mail-order and specialty pharmacies. The street math is consistent: brand rebates priced as a percentage of list (PBM retention estimated at 20 to 45 percent), generic spread pricing ($6 billed, $2 paid to the pharmacy, 30 cents acquisition cost), and one worked example extracting $175 gross from a single $1,000 specialty script. Practitioners split on remedies: transparent pass-through PBMs and carve-outs versus legislated delinking and fiduciary duties, with ERISA preemption already knocking back state reform in Oklahoma.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The baseline every speaker builds on is leverage through scale. KFF Health News traces how PBMs began in the late 1960s as claims processors and, after the FTC stepped in and drugmakers like Merck and Eli Lilly spun off their PBM holdings, consolidated until three players, CVS Caremark, Optum Rx and Express Scripts, control about 80 percent of the market [P21Zb_OySIg @ 00:01:43]. Dr. Eric Bricker of AHealthcareZ puts the figure at 85 percent and flags both the PBM layer and the three-wholesaler layer (McKesson, AmerisourceBergen, Cardinal) as oligopolies where the plan sponsor has very few options [vT0NNXYjQ_Y @ 00:04:36]. Tyler Dutchover explains why employers hand over the keys anyway: a 100-person company with four insulin users gets zero discount from a manufacturer, while a PBM negotiating for millions of prescriptions extracts major concessions [ufeHEzWD1Cc @ 00:04:08]. Vault of Profit frames the same moat from the owner's side: a PBM managing 1 million lives gets laughed out of the room with zero discounts, a PBM managing 100 million lives holds commercial life or death over a manufacturer's balance sheet, and no HR director will take the call unless the card works at 60,000 retail counters on day one [351RCg-LQ6I @ 00:04:13]. Scale is the entry ticket; everything else is built on top of it.

The second point of agreement is that the formulary is an auction and the rebate is the bid. STAT lays out the mechanic: drugmakers want tier 1 or tier 2 placement because that is where volume lives, so they offer the PBM a rebate, and the more expensive the list price, the higher the PBM's rebate tends to be [27INQuNycLA @ 00:02:27]. CancerCare states the incentive flatly: drugs with higher list prices can offer larger rebates, which can push a higher-priced drug into a preferred slot even when a lower-cost drug would be cheaper for the patient or the plan [f8oI5KtxoXM @ 00:01:56]. Audio Articles cites manufacturer rebates to PBMs climbing from $39.7 billion in 2012 to $89.5 billion in 2016 and notes that because rebates are calculated as a percentage of list price, high-deductible patients paying on list get hit harder [Cyz7QbHNjKc @ 00:02:11]. Tyler Dutchover runs the selection game with four insulin bids: the obvious lowest-price option loses, and the PBM picks Pharma Company 3 at a $300 sticker because it carries the biggest rebate, a $70 check split between PBM and client [ufeHEzWD1Cc @ 00:05:50]. The consistent read: the PBM's revenue rises with list price, so the auction rewards inflation rather than cheap net cost.

The third consensus pillar is that the money hides in contracts the buyer never sees. Benefits On The Fly sums up the three profit channels as spread pricing, retained rebates, and complex contracts where hidden fees and multiple revenue streams make it hard to track where the money actually goes [0ga6iJF0H1I @ 00:00:36]. Kendra Roberson of Faegre Drinker, speaking on the American Health Law Association podcast, defines spread pricing as the PBM charging the plan more than it pays the pharmacy and keeping the difference, and flags the Senate PBM Reform Act as proposing to prohibit it outright [bO0c-bD-CEA @ 00:13:15]. Audio Articles adds why it survives: the payment schedules PBMs generate for pharmacies are kept confidential from health plans, so the employer cannot compare what it paid against what the pharmacy received [Cyz7QbHNjKc @ 00:03:28]. Then comes vertical integration. Dr. Glaucomflecken's sketch has the insurer, the PBM and the pharmacy all turn out to be United Healthcare operating as Optum and Optum Rx, with every customer required to use the in-house pharmacy and the conglomerate boasting of 200 billion dollars a year [5rw4kNHNZyk @ 00:01:22]. The operator baseline: assume the PBM has a second customer, a pharmacy it owns, and a contract written so you cannot audit either.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Start with the brand rebate, because every speaker who runs the numbers lands on the same retention trick. Dr. Eric Bricker's illustrative case in AHealthcareZ: a $400 monthly brand, a $100 negotiated rebate, the PBM keeps $75 and tells the employer it secured a $25 rebate, which Bricker argues is really a commission dressed up as a discount [-xH2R8NZ4pU @ 00:13:37]. Bricker flags the figures as invented to show the principle, but the incentive holds: higher list prices mean bigger rebates and a bigger retained slice. Vault of Profit uses a $1,000 specialty carton: the manufacturer sends a $400 rebate per carton, the PBM announces it is passing 80 percent back, the employer receives $320 and the PBM keeps $80 as a rebate retention fee [351RCg-LQ6I @ 00:07:26]. Tyler Dutchover's insulin version shows the disclosure gap: the client is told it got a $50 rebate on a $300 drug, but the real check was $70 and the PBM quietly pocketed $20 [ufeHEzWD1Cc @ 00:07:26]. RxPreferred adds the formulary-exclusion angle: Tom's plan refuses a $20 generic antacid but covers $148 Nexium, the manufacturer pays a $50 rebate with $10 to the plan and $40 to the PBM, so the plan spends $138 instead of $20 [15IQO_jTMUM @ 00:03:22]. Same structure, four price points.

Spread is the second engine, and the numbers get sharper on generics. Bricker walks a generic with a $30 AWP: the PBM negotiates an 80 percent discount so the plan pays $6, pays the pharmacy a $2 maximum allowable cost (MAC), and keeps $4, while the pharmacy's actual acquisition cost, the NADAC, may be just 30 cents, leaving the pharmacy $1.70 [-xH2R8NZ4pU @ 00:16:24]. Bricker's punchline: AWP, the anchor for that 80 percent discount, stands for 'ain't what's paid', a number two quiet companies arguably make up. RxPreferred's spread game is blunter: the PBM pays the pharmacy $10, invoices the plan $100 plus a $2 admin fee, and nets $92 on one fill without the client knowing [15IQO_jTMUM @ 00:01:17]. Vault of Profit runs it on the $1,000 specialty script: the patient pays a $30 copay, the PBM pays the pharmacy $850, bills the employer $940, and captures a $90 spread; stack the $80 rebate retention and a $5 admin fee and the PBM extracts $175 gross without touching the box [351RCg-LQ6I @ 00:06:29]. Tyler Dutchover's insulin example: employer billed $250, pharmacy paid $200 take-it-or-leave-it under threat of network removal, a $50 spread on top of the $20 hidden rebate cut [ufeHEzWD1Cc @ 00:07:50].

The third layer runs through owned pharmacies. RxPreferred's repackaging game: the PBM pulls the plan and the member into its mail-order pharmacy with deeper discounts, a waived admin fee and lower copays, then repackages the drug and assigns its own AWP. The Lipitor fill that costs AWP $441 minus 15 percent plus a $2 fee, $376.85, at retail becomes AWP $684 minus 20 percent with no fee, $547.20, by mail, which RxPreferred calls technically legal but not ethical [15IQO_jTMUM @ 00:02:19]. Rujul Desai of Covington & Burling, on the American Health Law Association podcast, describes the specialty-pharmacy version: the PBM tells manufacturers to give larger discounts at its own pharmacy and lower rebates, because rebates must be passed along but pharmacy discounts stay with the owner [bO0c-bD-CEA @ 00:15:51]. Vault of Profit adds the back-end squeeze on independents: post-adjudication direct and indirect remuneration fees, where an automated audit months later claws back thousands from future remittances with no appeal, because the master contract was the only way to accept cards from 80 percent of the town [351RCg-LQ6I @ 00:10:55]. The counter-model SmithRx's Alan Pannier pitches is a PBM that owns no pharmacies or supply-chain assets and shows plan sponsors pharmacy contracts, manufacturer rebates and true drug cost through its Partner and Member Portals [KB9tHMlyhyA @ 00:00:55].

callout.title: How Practitioners Pry Open the PBM Black Box
callout.body: These are the specific questions, contract reads and structural moves the speakers use to find where the spread and retained rebates are hiding.
items: Ask the transparency question that actually matters: does the PBM have another customer besides the health plan? Demand disclosure of market share and bonus payments, not just rebates [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — vT0NNXYjQ_Y @ 00:04:07].

Read how 'rebate' is defined in any pass-through clause; Desai warns the definition has been narrowed over the years to create other pockets of revenue that escape a pass-through requirement [American Health Law Association — bO0c-bD-CEA @ 00:14:31].

If you are self-funded, carve out the PBM: fully insured plans are locked to the carrier's PBM, but self-funded sponsors run UnitedHealthcare medical with CVS Caremark or Express Scripts, or use a smaller PBM [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — -xH2R8NZ4pU @ 00:12:22].

Attack the formulary itself: target heavily advertised, low-efficacy drugs and move to evidence-proven medications that cost a fraction because they do not pay for Super Bowl ads [Benefits On The Fly — 0ga6iJF0H1I @ 00:02:12].

sop_steps.title: Map the seven players and both flows
sop_steps.action: Draw plan sponsor, plan, PBM, manufacturer, wholesaler, pharmacy and patient, then trace money one way and drugs the other.
sop_steps.detail: Bricker's standard is that a benefits operator can reproduce the PBM money-flow chart on a napkin and explain it in plain English before negotiating anything [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — vT0NNXYjQ_Y @ 00:01:08].

sop_steps.title: Demand full manufacturer-payment disclosure
sop_steps.action: Require the PBM to disclose rebates plus formulary, market penetration and bonus payments, and push for 100 percent pass-through.
sop_steps.detail: Benefits On The Fly's first move is partnering with a transparent PBM that passes 100 percent of manufacturer rebates and discounts to the plan sponsor, then using fee-discovery tools to surface what clients actually pay [Benefits On The Fly — 0ga6iJF0H1I @ 00:01:57].

sop_steps.title: Audit billed price against pharmacy paid price
sop_steps.action: Ask for what the PBM paid the pharmacy versus what it charged the plan, and benchmark generics against MAC and NADAC instead of AWP.
sop_steps.detail: Expect resistance: Dutchover reports PBMs can simply refuse, having written clauses calling the real drug cost a confidential trade secret, which is itself the signal that spread is in play [Tyler Dutchover — ufeHEzWD1Cc @ 00:09:52].

sop_steps.title: Restructure toward specialty control and flat fees
sop_steps.action: Concentrate on specialty spend and move to models with zero spread, zero retained rebates and flat per-script admin fees.
sop_steps.detail: Vault of Profit reports new competitors promising zero spread pricing, zero retained rebates and flat $5 administrative fees per script, the exact model large employers are defecting toward [Vault of Profit — 351RCg-LQ6I @ 00:12:47].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first fault line is whether the PBM toll is worth paying at all. STAT frames two camps directly: PBMs work with hospitals and insurers, carry a lot of people to negotiate for, and can push better prices for everybody, yet nobody outside the deal knows how much of the rebate reaches the consumer and the PBM could be pocketing a larger share [27INQuNycLA @ 00:02:47]. KFF Health News lands on a blunt yes and no: PBMs have helped keep some drug prices and premiums lower, but consumers do not see the savings directly, may be limited in drug choice, and prices for some drugs keep going up [P21Zb_OySIg @ 00:03:28]. Audio Articles adds the strongest pro-PBM data point, reporting that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services found larger negotiated rebates helped lower drug prices and slow spending growth over the last three years, while still flagging the percentage-of-list incentive [Cyz7QbHNjKc @ 00:01:17]. Benefits On The Fly takes the hard opposite line for employers: PBMs are just middlemen that evolved into major players profiting at your expense, and businesses with the right strategy are cutting pharmacy expenses by 30 to sometimes 50 percent [0ga6iJF0H1I @ 00:01:40]. Operators should treat the savings pitch and the extraction pitch as two sides they must price, not pick on faith.

The pass-through numbers themselves do not agree. Dr. Eric Bricker of AHealthcareZ pegs the share of manufacturer rebates passed to the plan at roughly 55 to 80 percent, with the PBM keeping 20 to 45 percent, and warns the manufacturer also pays formulary, market penetration and bonus payments outside the rebate line [vT0NNXYjQ_Y @ 00:03:31]. Audio Articles cites a study showing pass-through rising from 78 percent in 2012 to 91 percent in 2016, then immediately notes many small insurers and employers say they do not receive that share [Cyz7QbHNjKc @ 00:03:06]. Vault of Profit models an 80 percent pass-through on a $400 rebate, which still leaves the PBM $80 retained per carton before spread and admin fees are counted [351RCg-LQ6I @ 00:07:26]. The American Health Law Association panel explains why headline percentages mislead: Rujul Desai describes a narrowing and narrowing of the definition of rebate to create other pockets of revenue, so even a 100 percent pass-through mandate turns on how rebate gets defined [bO0c-bD-CEA @ 00:14:31]. The playbook split is clear: one camp audits the rebate percentage, the other audits every manufacturer payment stream, including discounts booked at a PBM-owned specialty pharmacy.

The biggest structural argument is whether to stay bundled, carve out, or go with a transparent independent. AHealthcareZ notes that if you are fully insured your PBM is tied to your carrier, but a self-funded plan can carve out the PBM, use a small independent, or even run a competing insurer's PBM, such as UnitedHealthcare medical with CVS Caremark or Express Scripts pharmacy [-xH2R8NZ4pU @ 00:12:22]. On specialty carve-outs, Bricker calls the question highly controversial, pointing to an OptumRx paper arguing a specialty carve-out PBM is a bad idea against a Pfizer presentation to the Dallas Fort Worth Business Group on Health arguing it is a good one [vT0NNXYjQ_Y @ 00:08:30]. SmithRx's Alan Pannier argues the opposite of scale-through-ownership: SmithRx owns no pharmacies or supply chain assets, which the company frames as what aligns incentives with plan sponsors and patients [KB9tHMlyhyA @ 00:00:55]. Vault of Profit argues the economics run the other way for anyone building a PBM, insisting you need at least 5 million covered lives before negotiating your first rebate contract and your own mail order and specialty network to capture the therapies driving 70 percent of pharmacy spend [351RCg-LQ6I @ 00:16:01].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most repeated firsthand trap is paying a fictitious price. RxPreferred walks through Tom's fill: the PBM paid the pharmacy $10, invoiced the plan $100 plus a $2 admin fee, so the plan paid $112 and the PBM kept $92 without its client's awareness [15IQO_jTMUM @ 00:01:17]. AHealthcareZ shows the generic version: a $30 AWP discounted 80 percent looks like a $6 win, but the PBM pays the pharmacy a $2 maximum allowable cost and the national average drug acquisition cost is 30 cents, which is why insiders say AWP stands for ain't what's paid [-xH2R8NZ4pU @ 00:16:24]. Vault of Profit runs the brand math on a $1,000 list specialty carton: the employer is billed $940, the pharmacy gets $850, and the $90 gap is spread taken with zero additional labor [351RCg-LQ6I @ 00:06:06]. Tyler Dutchover adds the insulin case where the employer is charged $250, the pharmacy is told to take $200 or leave the network, and the PBM pockets $50 on top of a $20 rebate skim, because neither side can see the other's contract [ufeHEzWD1Cc @ 00:07:39]. The check is simple: demand the pharmacy-paid amount per claim, not the AWP discount.

The rebate engine fails the payer by rewarding the expensive drug. RxPreferred's rebate game has Tom's plan refusing a $20 generic antacid but covering $148 Nexium; of a $50 manufacturer rebate, $10 goes to the plan and $40 returns to the PBM, so the plan spends $138 instead of $20 [15IQO_jTMUM @ 00:03:03]. AHealthcareZ calls the structure what it is: on a $400 brand with a $100 rebate, a PBM that keeps $75 and passes $25 is collecting a commission, which means it wants more prescriptions of higher-cost drugs and wants prices to go up [-xH2R8NZ4pU @ 00:13:37]. Tyler Dutchover plays the former drug company CEO testifying before Congress that bringing a product with a low list price gets you punished financially with no uptake, because everyone in the supply chain makes money on a higher list price [ufeHEzWD1Cc @ 00:08:46]. CancerCare spells out who eats it: the list price at the counter is often far higher than what the PBM or plan pays after rebates, which drives the copay and the out-of-pocket hit on high-deductible plans [f8oI5KtxoXM @ 00:02:31]. The economics check is net cost after rebate per therapeutic class, not the size of the rebate check.

The third trap lives in PBM-owned pharmacies. RxPreferred's repackaging game lures plan and member into mail order with deeper discounts and waived copays, then reassigns its own AWP: Lipitor at retail runs AWP $441 less 15 percent plus a $2 fee for $376.85, while repackaged mail order runs AWP $684 less 20 percent for $547.20 [15IQO_jTMUM @ 00:02:01]. The National Community Pharmacists Association's fill-my-pockets PBM character brags about forcing patients into a mail order pharmacy the PBM owns, lousy service or not, and says not even your pharmacist can do anything about it [lbfUr3FiuyU @ 00:01:40]. Rujul Desai of the American Health Law Association flags the self-dealing play: a PBM tells manufacturers to give larger discounts at its own specialty pharmacy and lower rebates, because rebates must be passed along but pharmacy discounts are kept [bO0c-bD-CEA @ 00:15:51]. Vault of Profit describes the pharmacy-side kill shot, retroactive direct and indirect remuneration fees clawed back months after dispensing through automated audits, with no court of appeal and no alternative network [351RCg-LQ6I @ 00:10:55]. Any model that routes specialty volume through an affiliated pharmacy needs a per-claim price comparison against retail before signing.

callout.title: Four Pre-Signature Kill Checks
callout.body: Run these before any PBM contract or renewal. Each one maps to a loss a practitioner documented on a real claim, rebate or contract clause.
items: Demand the actual pharmacy-paid amount next to the plan-billed amount on every claim; the $10 paid versus $100 billed case shows what an AWP-only invoice hides [RxPreferred — 15IQO_jTMUM @ 00:01:17].

Ask whether the PBM has another customer besides the health plan, and get formulary, market share and bonus payments disclosed, not just rebates [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — vT0NNXYjQ_Y @ 00:04:07].

Lock the contract definition of rebate to include all discounts and amounts based on a percentage of drug cost, because a narrowed definition creates new revenue pockets [American Health Law Association — bO0c-bD-CEA @ 00:14:31].
Strike any clause calling real drug costs confidential trade secrets; if the PBM can refuse to show the receipts, assume you are paying more than needed [Tyler Dutchover — ufeHEzWD1Cc @ 00:09:52].

action_checklist: Learn the seven-player money flow cold, plan sponsor, health plan, PBM, manufacturer, wholesaler, pharmacy and patient, until you can redraw it on a napkin (AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained, vT0NNXYjQ_Y @ 00:00:50).
If self-funded, carve the PBM out of the medical carrier and bid small independents or a competing insurer's PBM (AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained, -xH2R8NZ4pU @ 00:12:22).

Partner with a transparent PBM that passes 100 percent of manufacturer rebates and discounts to the plan sponsor, and run fee-discovery tools to surface hidden PBM fees (Benefits On The Fly, 0ga6iJF0H1I @ 00:01:57).
Push for a flat, non-percentage fee per claim so PBM compensation is delinked from drug price, rebate retention and spread (American Health Law Association, bO0c-bD-CEA @ 00:16:42).
Audit the formulary for low-efficacy, heavily advertised drugs and steer to evidence-proven medications that cost a fraction as much (Benefits On The Fly, 0ga6iJF0H1I @ 00:02:12).

Check generic cash prices against the copay, since a $1.80 cash cream beat a $10 copay, and use first-line generics like methotrexate before jumping to specialty drugs (AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained, -xH2R8NZ4pU @ 00:04:25).

chapters.question_prompt: How do self-funded employers spot PBM spread, rebate, and MAC games in their contracts, and how do pharmacies survive PBM audits?
chapters.title: PBM Contract Forensics: Spread, Rebates, MAC Pricing, and Audits
chapters.subtitle: Generic spread pricing, rebate pass-through definitions, maximum allowable cost indexes, transparent and pass-through contract language, generic compliance ratios, continuous pricing improvement, specialty carve-outs, and PBM audit and network compliance
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners converge on one diagnosis: the PBM profits in the gap between what the plan is billed and what the pharmacy is paid, and percentage discounts off AWP hide that gap. Dr. Eric Bricker's amlodipine math shows a plan paying 48 cents for a drug acquired at 1.9 cents, roughly 25 times cost, while Jim Lodge cites an almost 500% markup in the Johnson & Johnson case. Rebate pass-through pledges leak through PBM-owned GPOs and rebate aggregators, and rebates fell from 48% to 13% of PBM profit. Operators fight back with absolute-price benchmarks, quarterly discount audits that recover 10 to 40%, five core contract clauses, and specialty carve-outs. Practitioners split on whether pass-through contracts fix the problem or simply move it: SmithRx and Cora Opsahl argue that fixed guarantees still trap sponsors inside pass-through deals.

key_metrics.label: Generic Spread Multiplier
key_metrics.context: Amlodipine (generic Norvasc) walk-through: AWP $2.38 at 20% of AWP is 48 cents billed to the plan, the pharmacy acquires the drug for 1.9 cents, and the plan pays almost exactly 25 times more.

key_metrics.label: High-Cost Drug Markup in J&J Fiduciary Case
key_metrics.metric: High-Cost Drug Markup in J&J Fiduciary Case
key_metrics.context: High-cost drugs were marked up an average of almost 500% to Johnson & Johnson compared with pharmacy reimbursement, and the PBM kept the spread as pure profit on top of admin fees.

key_metrics.label: Rebates as Share of PBM Profit
key_metrics.metric: Rebates as Share of PBM Profit
key_metrics.context: Nephron profit mix: admin fees rose from 5% to 22% and mail/specialty/spread rose from 47% to 65%, so 100% rebate pass-through touches only 13% of profit and leaves 87% outside it.

key_metrics.label: PBM Audit Overcharge Findings
key_metrics.context: A jumbo plan sponsor reports that audits find 30 to 40% overcharges and that every audit the sponsor has run yielded money back; The Partners Group puts typical audit findings at 10 to 30%.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Spread pricing is not complex, whatever the PBM pitch about puts and takes. Jim Lodge of PBM Insider breaks it into two contracts. The first is the PBM-to-plan-sponsor contract, which carries the formulary, the prices and the estimated rebates. The second is a separate PBM-to-pharmacy contract that pays a drug reimbursement plus a professional dispensing fee. Spread pricing is simply the difference between the two [o57C9bK5ouI @ 00:00:59]. Dr. Eric Bricker of AHealthcareZ reduces it to two formulas. PBM profit equals the net AWP billed to the plan minus MAC plus dispensing fee. Pharmacy profit equals MAC plus fee minus acquisition cost from the wholesaler [0XFk1m3yGuY @ 00:01:34]. Gary Alton of The Partners Group sees the same gap at the carrier level, where a carrier negotiates a 75% discount, passes along 65% and keeps a 10-point spread [Cxvmh46o824 @ 00:43:34]. Lodge anchors the stakes in the Johnson & Johnson fiduciary case, where high-cost drugs were marked up almost 500% over pharmacy reimbursement and the PBM kept the difference as pure profit on top of its admin fees [o57C9bK5ouI @ 00:01:20]. The remedy Lodge prescribes is blunt: the sponsor pays the identical ingredient cost and dispensing fee the PBM reimburses the pharmacy, and the admin fee is the PBM's only revenue.

The second point of agreement: a discount off AWP is not a price. On Relentless Health Value, the Gleevec example from Benjamin Jolley runs the numbers. Branded Gleevec cost $27,000 a month. Generic imatinib through a PBM cost $9,000 a month and was framed as an $18,000 savings. The Cost Plus cash price was $25 a month. AWP means Ain't What's Paid, so sponsors should insist on absolute prices rather than discounts [xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:08:26]. Justine of TheCoyPharmer explains why the guarantee works as a floor. If the sponsor was promised AWP minus 89% and the book runs at minus 88%, the PBM pays the shortfall, but overperformance is not reciprocal, because PBM guarantees to plan sponsors are typically a minimum level [H3p5Yw0Y-ek @ 00:07:20]. Alan Pannier of SmithRx extends the critique to pass-through deals. Under both spread and pass-through models, the PBM is incentivized to manage pricing toward the fixed rates set at selection, so better pharmacy and manufacturer pricing won mid-term never reaches the sponsor [ZuvAxUS0mII @ 00:00:30]. Cora Opsahl adds that guarantees are reconciled by therapeutic category at year end, with figures like AWP minus 49 reverse-engineered after the fact [xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:14:09].

Practitioners also agree that a 100% rebate pass-through pledge settles very little. Dr. Bricker lists the pledges: Optum in January 2025, CVS in 2018, and Cigna/Express Scripts in October 2025, effective 2027. Then Bricker points to the PBM-owned GPOs (Optum's MSR, CVS's Zinc, Cigna's Ascent), which collect admin fees that are a total black box [yFJFnewKqw4 @ 00:03:01]. Using Nephron figures, Bricker shows the profit mix shifting between 2012 and 2023. Rebates fell from 48% to 13% of PBM profit. Admin fees rose from 5% to 22%, and mail, specialty and spread rose from 47% to 65%. A pass-through promise therefore touches only 13% of profit and leaves 87% outside it [yFJFnewKqw4 @ 00:08:25]. Frier Levitt describes litigation-exposed rebate aggregators that demand, for example, 25 cents on the dollar for formulary access. The aggregator keeps about 30% and passes 60 to 70 cents to the PBM, which then tells the plan it is turning it all over [8mubYuuHvMI @ 00:01:20]. Benefits Blake supplies the scoreboard: only 59% of employers receive full traditional rebates, and only 57% receive full specialty rebates [wUzyX8bEvt0 @ 00:11:06].

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Bricker's amlodipine walk-through is the template for repricing a generic claim. AWP for generic Norvasc is $2.38, and at an 80% discount the plan pays the PBM 20%, or 48 cents [0XFk1m3yGuY @ 00:02:14]. MAC is unknown, not published and proprietary, so Bricker plugs in a hypothetical 25 cents for MAC plus dispensing fee. On those numbers the PBM keeps 23 cents. The pharmacy buys the drug for 1.9 cents and also clears about 23 cents. The plan pays almost exactly 25 times more than the drug costs [0XFk1m3yGuY @ 00:03:09]. Scaled up, Ohio Medicaid lost $208 million on generic spend alone, and Kentucky Medicaid had the same problem. That raises the question of what is happening inside municipalities, school systems and private employers [0XFk1m3yGuY @ 00:03:27]. Alton's case study of an employer with roughly 400 lives answers it for the private side. The effective generic discount was 55% under the incumbent versus 76% under the C2 coalition contract, and rebate shares across the market ranged from 0% to 75 to 80% [Cxvmh46o824 @ 00:51:42]. The switch was projected to save 30%, or $163K, and came in at about 32%.

MAC is where the generic spread is manufactured. Justine, a pharmacist with 20 years in the field, explains that brand claims reimburse at a stable AWP minus 18 to 21%. Generics instead run on MAC prices that the PBM sets unilaterally and changes by member, by network or over time. A claim with a $45 usual and customary price is paid at MAC whenever MAC is lower [H3p5Yw0Y-ek @ 00:04:54]. Behind the scenes there are separate MAC lists for each pharmacy guarantee. Sponsors are grouped into 5 to 8 cohorts, the lists are adjusted daily or weekly, and overperforming sponsors may be migrated to a new MAC list [H3p5Yw0Y-ek @ 00:13:52]. PA Pharmacists document the pharmacy side. One drug's cost jumped from $25 to $155 while MAC reimbursement sat at $55, a $100 loss on the fill. The pharmacy lost at least $1,500 in two weeks, because PBMs cut MAC quickly but lag on increases [l81CzyzPR6M @ 00:01:11]. Cora Opsahl reports the pass-through version of the squeeze. Plans are charged on an AWP discount while pharmacies are reimbursed on acquisition cost plus. GLP-1 claims come in roughly $130 underwater, so pharmacies refuse those scripts [xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:13:20].

The contracting and audit cadence practitioners run is concrete. Alton's C2 coalition is 7 firms with $3.3B of premium under management. It sent an RFP to 13 PBMs, received 8 responses to more than 350 questions, and selected Express Scripts and CVS Caremark. It renegotiates contracts annually and audits discounts quarterly [Cxvmh46o824 @ 00:09:35]. On fees, Alton sees integration charges from $0.45 to $6 PEPM and pegs a reasonable fee at $2 to $3. A mandatory mail-order program would add about 5% more savings [Cxvmh46o824 @ 00:46:05]. Benefits Blake reduces the contract to five clauses: rebate pass-through, a spread ban, audit rights (30 days' notice is tolerable), data ownership and fee disclosure. Blake adds a warning not to evaluate a PBM on its pitch deck [wUzyX8bEvt0 @ 00:09:10]. Cora Opsahl names the fine print that blunts audits: pre-approved auditors, 250-claim samples, no extrapolation and a limited look-back. There is also the contractual bar that stops a sponsor from auditing its own claims. Even so, every audit Cora has run yielded money back, with overcharges of 30 to 40% [xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:17:14].

callout.title: Leverage plays practitioners use against PBM contract terms
callout.body: These are the moves practitioners say shift negotiating power back to the plan sponsor, from RFP design to specialty carve-outs [Relentless Health Value — xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:18:34].
items: Make the RFP require Cost Plus Drugs in the network. Cuban says the big PBMs will immediately offer bigger rebates and better terms to try to keep Cost Plus out [Relentless Health Value — xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:18:34].

Negotiate all the way down to the definitions section with competent counsel, and do not use consultants paid by the PBM, which Frier Levitt calls a real conflict of interest [Frier Levitt — 8mubYuuHvMI @ 00:03:34].
Ask for monthly or weekly reporting, and push toward NADAC or pass-through pricing so that overperformance on MAC flows to the sponsor rather than the PBM [TheCoyPharmer — H3p5Yw0Y-ek @ 00:15:25].

Carve out specialty starting with one biosimilar switch. Purdue moved Remicade to Inflectra for about 32% year-over-year savings, met with nearly every affected member, and now adds drugs quarterly [Employers' Forum of Indiana — zoRFywXBoLM @ 00:17:56].

sop_steps.title: Map both contracts and reprice generic claims
sop_steps.action: Lay the sponsor contract next to the pharmacy reimbursement terms and compute the PBM margin on each claim.
sop_steps.detail: Treat spread as the difference between the PBM-to-sponsor and PBM-to-pharmacy contracts, then apply the formula PBM profit = net AWP minus (MAC plus dispensing fee). Run it on generics such as amlodipine, where 48 cents is billed for a drug bought at 1.9 cents [PBM Insider — o57C9bK5ouI @ 00:00:21] [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — 0XFk1m3yGuY @ 00:01:34].

sop_steps.title: Benchmark generic performance against absolute numbers
sop_steps.action: Check the generic dispense rate and the effective generic discount against coalition-level rates.
sop_steps.detail: A generic dispense rate in the mid-70s is a red flag. An effective generic discount of 55% against a 76% coalition rate shows how much money is on the table before renewal [The Partners Group — Cxvmh46o824 @ 00:15:36] [The Partners Group — Cxvmh46o824 @ 00:51:42].

sop_steps.title: Rewrite the contract around five clauses and tight definitions
sop_steps.action: Insert rebate pass-through, a spread ban, audit rights, data ownership and fee disclosure, and define GPO admin fees inside pass-through.
sop_steps.detail: Benefits Blake's five clauses form the spine of the contract, with 30 days' audit notice as tolerable. Pass-through language must reach the GPO admin fees that Bricker calls a total black box [Benefits Blake — wUzyX8bEvt0 @ 00:09:10] [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — yFJFnewKqw4 @ 00:03:01].

sop_steps.title: Audit quarterly and re-bid annually
sop_steps.action: Run quarterly discount audits and strike audit limits such as fixed claim samples and no-extrapolation clauses.
sop_steps.detail: C2 audits discounts quarterly and renegotiates annually. Typical audits find 10 to 30%, and Cora Opsahl reports 30 to 40% overcharges and money back on every audit run [The Partners Group — Cxvmh46o824 @ 00:56:10] [Relentless Health Value — xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:16:37].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Jim Lodge's fix for spread is blunt: the plan sponsor should pay the PBM the exact ingredient cost and dispensing fee the PBM pays the pharmacy, leaving the admin fee as the PBM's only revenue, which Lodge calls “just the correct and transparent way to do things” [o57C9bK5ouI @ 00:01:59]. Dr. Eric Bricker argues that headline pass-through pledges miss where the money moved. Using Nephron data, Bricker shows rebates fell from 48% of PBM profit in 2012 to 13% in 2023, while admin fees rose to 22% and mail, specialty and spread climbed to 65%, so a 100% rebate pass-through covers only 13% of the profit pool and leaves 87% outside it [yFJFnewKqw4 @ 00:08:25]. Alan Pannier at SmithRx goes further, warning that under both spread and pass-through models the PBM is incentivized to manage pricing toward the fixed discount rates the sponsor locked in at selection [ZuvAxUS0mII @ 00:00:30]. Cora Opsahl, running a jumbo plan, describes the same mismatch from inside a so-called pass-through deal: the plan gets charged on an AWP discount while pharmacies get reimbursed on acquisition cost plus, and the guarantees are reconciled by therapeutic category at year end [xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:12:47]. The operator takeaway: the label on the contract settles nothing until the pricing formula on both sides matches.

The Partners Group plays the incumbent game and keeps score in discounts. Gary Alton's C2 coalition, seven firms with $3.3B in premium, ran a 350-question RFP across 13 PBMs and landed on Express Scripts and CVS Caremark; in the roughly 400-life case study, the client's effective generic discount was 55% against 76% under C2, with rebate shares across the market ranging from 0% up to 75-80% [Cxvmh46o824 @ 00:51:42]. The Relentless Health Value panel attacks that whole scoreboard. Citing Benjamin Jolley, they walk through imatinib: branded Gleevec at $27,000 a month, PBM generic at $9,000 framed as an “$18,000 savings,” and a Cost Plus cash price of $25 a month, concluding that AWP means “Ain't What's Paid” and buyers should insist on absolute prices instead of discounts [xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:08:26]. Cuban's alternative lever is to stop playing on the big PBMs' turf: write the RFP so Cost Plus Drugs must be in the network, and the incumbents “will immediately give you a better deal to try to exclude us” [xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:18:34]. Benefits Blake points to the same exit ramp, listing Cost Plus at a 15% markup and transparent shops like Capital Rx, SmithRx, Navitus, Rightway and FairosRx as live replacements for the Big Three [wUzyX8bEvt0 @ 00:05:48].

On specialty, the split is carve it out versus fix the pricing engine in place. Candace Schaefer at Purdue carved specialty to Archimedes after seeing specialty eat 46% of Rx dollars on 1-2% of volume; the first move, Remicade to the biosimilar Inflectra, was projected to save about $180K and actually landed near 32% year over year, and Purdue now adds drugs quarterly [zoRFywXBoLM @ 00:17:56]. Robert Lewis of Rx Benefits backs the carve-out direction with trend data: carved-in pharmacy running 10-12% against 3-4% carved out, with 85% of the Fortune 500 already carved out versus about 1 in 5 mid-market employers [Cxvmh46o824 @ 00:34:06]. Justine at TheCoyPharmer keeps the fight inside the pricing index instead, arguing that NADAC or pass-through models are what let generic overperformance flow back to the sponsor rather than stay with the PBM's MAC spread [H3p5Yw0Y-ek @ 00:14:30]. Alan Pannier pitches a third route: platform pricing where new pharmacy network and manufacturer contracts are applied immediately and visible in real time across the whole book, instead of renegotiating fixed rates [ZuvAxUS0mII @ 00:01:17]. Each path attacks the same leak, but carve-outs demand heavy member contact, while index or platform fixes depend on reporting visibility.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first sponsor-side trap is the stale contract. Gary Alton watched a multi-year deal freeze a client into “stale discounts,” with one exit penalty topping $500K, and in the same case study a carrier negotiated 75% but passed along 65%, quietly keeping a 10% spread [Cxvmh46o824 @ 00:44:25]. Alton puts typical audit findings at 10-30%, the size of leak a frozen contract can hide. Alan Pannier explains why the lock hurts even without fraud: over the term the PBM keeps winning better retail pharmacy and manufacturer pricing, but the sponsor gets none of those gains because its pricing is fixed [ZuvAxUS0mII @ 00:01:02]. Justine at TheCoyPharmer flags the trap inside the guarantee itself: PBM guarantees to plan sponsors are “typically a minimum level,” so a sponsor promised AWP minus 89% that runs at minus 88% gets the shortfall paid [H3p5Yw0Y-ek @ 00:07:20]. The catch is that the PBM runs separate MAC lists per guarantee, groups sponsors into 5-8 cohorts, adjusts the lists daily or weekly, and may migrate an overperforming sponsor onto a new MAC list [H3p5Yw0Y-ek @ 00:13:52]. The economics check is simple: without the monthly or weekly reporting Justine tells resellers to demand, a sponsor cannot tell whether its contractual floor quietly became its ceiling.

On rebates, the trap is believing the pass-through promise without seeing the plumbing. Frier Levitt describes litigation that exposed PBM-owned rebate aggregators demanding, say, 25 cents on the dollar for formulary access, keeping about 30% and sending 60-70 cents to the PBM, which then tells the plan “we're going to turn it all over to you” [8mubYuuHvMI @ 00:01:20]. Frier Levitt adds that Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage carry reporting duties while ERISA private plans have no such obligation, so the private employer sees only what the contract forces [8mubYuuHvMI @ 00:02:16]. Benefits Blake puts a number on the damage: only 59% of employers receive full traditional rebates and 57% full specialty rebates [wUzyX8bEvt0 @ 00:11:06]. The second trap is the referee. Frier Levitt calls consultants paid by the PBM a “real conflict of interest,” and Cora Opsahl's panel describes big PBMs paying consultants per RFP while renewals get pitched as “only up 4% or 6%” [xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:16:01]. Even the audit right gets hollowed out with pre-approved auditors, 250-claim samples, no extrapolation and limited look-back, and the panel notes a sponsor must hire an outside auditor because doing it in-house would violate the contract, even though audits in that world find 30-40% overcharges.

On the pharmacy side, the failure modes are cash-flow bleeds and audit compounding. A PA Pharmacists speaker filled a drug whose cost jumped from $25 to $155 against a $55 MAC, a $100 loss on one fill, and lost at least $1,500 in two weeks because PBMs cut MAC prices fast but lag on increases [l81CzyzPR6M @ 00:01:11]. Frier Levitt's team says the top audit discrepancy is inventory shortage, and some PBMs reconcile at the NDC level, so buying a 50-count package against a 100-count billed NDC reads as a shortage and can trigger full recovery [67He43cmPRc @ 00:17:51]. Frier Levitt's New Jersey panel warns that shrugging off a $5,000 finding burns pharmacies later: findings compound, as in $5,000 in 2021 and $25,000 in 2023 feeding a 2025 network review, so every finding gets appealed regardless of size [hKqVi489zow @ 00:14:40]. Late fixes backfire too. Collecting house-account copays only after an audit notice lands is a “red flag” [67He43cmPRc @ 00:28:44], and copay evidence produced after the audit starts gets rejected. The economics check: a $10,000 audit you ignore is the down payment on a termination, and a MAC price you never appeal keeps bleeding margin until the list finally moves.

callout.title: Hard Stops Before You Sign, Renew, or Settle
callout.body: Four stops drawn straight from the money practitioners watched sponsors and pharmacies lose.
items: Do not accept a pass-through label until the plan's charge basis matches pharmacy reimbursement; Cora Opsahl reports AWP-discount billing against acquisition-cost-plus reimbursement [Relentless Health Value — xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:12:47].
Do not sign a multi-year deal without annual repricing; stale discounts and an exit penalty above $500K trapped one client [The Partners Group — Cxvmh46o824 @ 00:44:25].
Do not let a 100% rebate pass-through pledge end diligence; PBM-owned GPO admin fees remain a total black box [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — yFJFnewKqw4 @ 00:03:01].
Do not send purchase records for the listed claims only or skip a small audit; submit every purchase source for the full period [Frier Levitt — hKqVi489zow @ 00:06:59].

action_checklist: Rewrite the contract so the PBM charges the same ingredient cost and dispensing fee it pays the pharmacy, with the admin fee as its only revenue [PBM Insider — o57C9bK5ouI @ 00:01:59].
Price drugs in absolute dollars instead of AWP discounts, checking PBM generics against the $25 Cost Plus imatinib benchmark [Relentless Health Value — xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:08:26].
Write Cost Plus Drugs into the RFP network requirement to force incumbents into a better deal [Relentless Health Value — xHAyQelFkf8 @ 00:18:34].
Lock in the five clauses: rebate pass-through, spread ban, audit rights with tolerable 30-day notice, data ownership, and fee disclosure [Benefits Blake — wUzyX8bEvt0 @ 00:09:10].
Renegotiate annually, audit discounts quarterly, and expect typical audit findings of 10-30% [The Partners Group — Cxvmh46o824 @ 00:56:10].
On the pharmacy side, self-audit regularly and keep independent purchase records from every wholesaler before any audit notice arrives [Frier Levitt — 67He43cmPRc @ 00:53:08].

chapters.question_prompt: How does reference-based pricing and direct contracting replace PPO network discounts, and how are balance bills and provider pushback handled?
chapters.title: Reference-Based Pricing and Direct Contracting
chapters.subtitle: RBP vs. PPO and commercial claims pricing, Medicare-plus pricing, chargemasters, negotiation best practices, surprise-billing interaction, member advocacy, RBP costs, and direct employer–provider contracts
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree reference-based pricing is just a different way to pay a claim inside a self-funded or level-funded plan: build up from Medicare instead of discounting down from a hospital chargemaster. Quoted savings run 20 to 40 percent, and ClaimDOC reports a 300-employee agricultural group cutting plan spend 41.4 percent, from $819 to $480 per employee per month, with zero known balance bills. The street mechanics: pay facilities the greater of Medicare plus 25 or cost plus 20, clinically audit every inpatient bill, pre-sign physicians through outreach that wins 95 percent acceptance, and cut single-case agreements on the rest. Operators split on posture, from Montana's arm-twisting that cut hospital pay to 200-220 percent of Medicare, to pay-and-defend versus negotiate-and-settle, while one producer reverted a client to PPO within months over balance-bill complaints.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who prices claims for a living lands on the same core mechanic: reference-based pricing is not a plan, it is a different way to pay a claim. Lester Morales frames the PPO as top-down, starting from a hospital's billed charge and shaving a discount, while RBP is bottom-up, starting from Medicare and paying a percentage above it, with both routes answering the same question of what the plan reimburses for a knee surgery or an MRI [xVuFXA-gN8g @ 00:05:18]. Omar Arif of ClaimDOC goes further, calling the product network replacement rather than RBP, and pointing out that every big carrier already reference-prices out-of-network claims and already pays physicians Medicare plus a markup, so RBP is baked into every group plan in the country [A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:22:42]. Tom Stein of American Trust Administrators strips the chargemaster down to a restaurant menu that only the uninitiated believe is real, and says RBP discounts that menu entirely and keys off what the hospital accepts from its biggest payer, the government [D3AuT-Ki3nw @ 00:02:52]. Mike Kupa of Remodel Benefits calls the savings 'literally just math': egregious providers sitting inside carrier contracts simply get paid less, and that gap is where the employer's money comes back [vCzjI43ZWVI @ 00:03:26].

The savings bands cluster tightly across operators who run the numbers independently. Kupa tells employers to expect 20 to 30 percent on medical spend, sometimes more, after years of implementing and maintaining RBP plans [vCzjI43ZWVI @ 00:00:49]. Arif says ClaimDOC has historically promised 25 to 35 percent of overall spend depending on geography and plan structure, and that its 2022 book was tracking into the high 30s or low 40s against Kaiser Family Foundation figures, measured on true cost per employee and per family rather than on discount percentages [A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:37:45]. The funding prerequisite is just as uniform. Howard Deihl of The General Agency states RBP contracts are only written self-funded or level-funded, never in the fully insured market, are medically underwritten, and in the level-funded version unused claim funds get refunded to the employer, so low utilization stacks extra savings on top of the rate cut [FPcS3pupwwA @ 00:05:33]. Ryan of Holloway Benefit Concepts confirms underwriting and risk analysis still apply, pitches the model squarely at small and mid-sized businesses, and reports two clients on RBP whose claim costs and overall premiums dropped two years in a row [2dsXkvZasDU @ 00:01:14]. Deihl adds that RBP coinsurance can run anywhere from 50 to 90 percent, but the single out-of-pocket maximum is the number operators sell on.

The third consensus point is that RBP fails without member education and advocacy wrapped around it. Rhett Robbins says employees can visit virtually any provider but need to confirm in advance that the provider accepts RBP pricing, with a third-party advocate stepping in to negotiate any billing dispute, and folds direct contracting with preferred providers into the same toolkit [8begy-typh4 @ 00:01:24]. Benefits Studio names the two catches every buyer has to price in: without a contract a hospital can balance bill the employee for the rest of its charge, and some hospitals refuse to take part at all, which leaves real gaps in access [noY8cLblMi4 @ 00:01:31]. Arif is blunt that nobody saves a health plan 20 to 40, sometimes 50 percent without disruption, and that the fix is telling clients up front what will break and how it gets fixed, then repeating it in a constant drip of communication all year [mPaz9R2yMrs @ 00:08:48]. Marty Makary, in a clip run by both Imagine360 and ELAP, supplies the macro case operators lean on when the noise starts: hospital prices have no orbit, they need to be anchored to something, and reference-based pricing is that anchor, with the added promise of reining in surprise billing and ensuring claims are paid at a fair amount [U6ZwMY7UtFU @ 00:02:01].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The rate engine is where operators make or lose the deal. ClaimDOC prices every facility claim two ways, Medicare plus a 25 percent markup and the hospital's own self-reported cost plus a 20 percent markup, then pays whichever is higher; the cost figure comes from the cost-of-services report every Medicare hospital must file with CMS, which Arif argues is fully loaded because hospitals use it to set their own government reimbursement [mPaz9R2yMrs @ 00:24:54]. The math runs line by line, so the plan can defend every payment as fair and reasonable, and Arif, self-described as aggressive, says a flat-Medicare program a broker touted on LinkedIn would scare even Arif [A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:48:56]. Kupa's worked example shows where the spread lives: a $10,000 billed procedure with a 62.5 percent carrier discount pays $3,750, roughly 250 percent of Medicare; Medicare itself pays $1,500; an RBP plan at 150 percent pays $2,250, an effective 77.5 percent discount [vCzjI43ZWVI @ 00:01:46]. Deihl gives the carrier comparison operators quote against, with insurers averaging about 140 percent of Medicare for hospital services and 120 to 125 percent for physician services, higher or lower depending on the carrier [FPcS3pupwwA @ 00:00:41].

Access is engineered before the first claim drops. ClaimDOC's Pave the Way program pulls the consultant's top utilization report, lets members nominate their own doctors during open enrollment and all year, then calls each office with a fixed script: here is how we pay, how fast we pay, the payer ID, what the card looks like, and will you keep charging the $25 copay; that outreach lands about a 95 percent physician acceptance rate [mPaz9R2yMrs @ 00:12:17]. Facility care is left to flow through normal pre-certification: Arif estimates roughly 85 percent of outpatient procedures clear with no friction, eight or nine of every ten flagged cases settle through a ten-person provider relations team run by a former hospital executive, leaving one or two percent that need a delay or a redirect to another facility [mPaz9R2yMrs @ 00:21:38]. In markets locked by one dominant system, the plan B is contracting freestanding ambulatory surgery centers, while ERs stay covered because the Consolidated Appropriations Act bars them from balance billing the member [A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:38:40]. Eric Bricker's direct-contracting stack mirrors this: bundled or discounted fee-for-service rates, an independent TPA loading a client-specific network, zero out-of-pocket benefit design, and a navigation service [xcu6bvj22fc @ 00:02:50].

The back end is a claims-defense machine. Arif relays the ClaimDOC CEO's estimate that the clinical team of nurses and coding experts scrapes 25 to 30 percent of the dollars off any inpatient stay before repricing even starts [A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:33:00]. The marquee catch is ICU unbundling: Arif cites Stanford billing up to $80,000 a day for what should be an all-in per diem, and COVID-era claims where oxygen, ventilator, ECMO and even nursing were split out until bills hit $23 million and tripped PPO outlier clauses, turning a presumed 50 percent discount into 15 percent [mPaz9R2yMrs @ 00:35:26]. Every audited facility claim goes to the hospital by certified mail with appeal instructions and the hospital's own self-reported financials; if the provider later bills the member, a notice goes to that same address stating the check was cashed and the plan paid per the plan document. ClaimDOC itself is paid a percentage of billed charge, capped per claim, and Arif says experienced stop-loss carriers grant ClaimDOC decrements that more than offset the fee against a fixed-PEPM vendor [A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:34:41]. Deihl's carriers go one step further on collections, mailing providers a letter telling them not to report the member while a claims negotiation runs [FPcS3pupwwA @ 00:07:38].

callout.title: Leverage Plays the Operators Actually Use
callout.body: These are the specific pressure points practitioners pulled to get hospitals, physicians, and members to accept a Medicare-anchored price.
items: Rational analysis alone did not close Montana; the deal closed after threats to publish commercial payment rates and the personal emails and cell numbers of hospital board members, CEOs and CFOs, plus union pressure and an offer to ship members out of state with free transportation [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — gpm3vtKEf5U @ 00:03:19].

Target reimbursement sandwiched between government and commercial payers so a nonprofit system cannot credibly call the payment unfair when it beats their biggest payer [Dysrupt Healthcare Podcast — mPaz9R2yMrs @ 00:27:32].

Run a dual option on the UMR and United network: ClaimDOC's first case offered a $2,000 deductible at $130 a month versus $200 a month for United, and 350 enrolled with ClaimDOC while six picked United [Self-Funded — A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:55:41].

In direct contracting, the bargaining chips are concentrated headcount for steerage and faster payment, since major carriers can take 30, 60, even 90 days to pay the provider [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — xcu6bvj22fc @ 00:02:17].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first fault line is the multiple itself. Ryan at Holloway Benefit Concepts sells plans where every claim is paid at a higher percentage of Medicare, typically 150% to 200%, and pitches it as an exit from back-door, no-transparency carrier-hospital negotiations [2dsXkvZasDU @ 00:00:24]. Omar Arif at ClaimDOC runs a tighter, line-by-line formula: facilities get Medicare plus 25% or the hospital's own self-reported cost plus 20%, whichever is higher, and that floor is what lets ClaimDOC defend every payment as fair and reasonable. Arif says a broker moving a client to flat Medicare would scare even an operator as aggressive as Arif [A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:48:56]. Howard Deihl at The General Agency puts the incumbent baseline on the table: carriers are reimbursing about 140% of Medicare for hospital services and 120% to 125% for physician services, with some higher and some lower depending on the carrier [FPcS3pupwwA @ 00:00:41]. Tom Stein at American Trust Administrators attacks from the opposite flank, arguing that paying 50% more than the state pays means small business is getting fleeced, while hospitals counter that government underpayment forces private plans to subsidize them [D3AuT-Ki3nw @ 00:03:28]. Same chassis, different price anchors, and each one moves acceptance, savings, and defensibility in a different direction.

Negotiation posture splits practitioners even harder. Arif lays out the two primary ways to run RBP: pay and defend, where the plan pays what it judges fair and defends the claim, or negotiate and settle, which can be better for a member in certain scenarios but sets a bad precedent and dilutes plan assets. ClaimDOC keeps both weapons plus single case agreements and direct contracts under one roof, with legal, provider relations, and member services in-house [A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:29:51]. Dr. Eric Bricker at AHealthcareZ argues rational analysis alone did not seal the deal in Montana: Marilyn Bartlett's analysis found Medicare covered 92% of hospital costs, yet the agreement only closed after arm twisting, including threats to publish commercial payment rates and the personal cell phone numbers of hospital board members, CEOs, and CFOs [gpm3vtKEf5U @ 00:03:19]. Bricker's direct-contracting playbook runs on volume instead of threats: a concentrated workforce gives the employer steerage as leverage at the table with independent physician practices and ambulatory surgery centers [xcu6bvj22fc @ 00:01:02]. Carrie Nixon at Healthcare Solutions Connection reports Boeing going straight to two local accountable care organizations in Puget Sound, where 30% of employees chose the preferred partnership option in year one with an 8.5 out of 10 satisfaction rating [ypiI6d2Bnkk @ 00:01:53].

The fee model and the rollout architecture are the third split. Arif defends ClaimDOC taking a percentage of billed charge, capped per claim, over a flat fee: on a 200-life case where nobody hits the hospital for six months, the employer pays $30 PEPM to a fixed-fee vendor or nothing to ClaimDOC, and stop-loss carriers that know the model hand out decrements [A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:34:13]. Benefits Studio counters that there is no public price list, every TPA and RBP vendor fee is quoted, and Willis Towers Watson warns repricing fees can eat into the saving [noY8cLblMi4 @ 00:01:12]. On architecture, Arif rejects RBP ever becoming the norm and expects a hybrid with PPOs; ClaimDOC already runs dual-option enrollments, and on the first one six employees picked the United Healthcare plan while 350 picked ClaimDOC at a lower monthly premium [A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:55:41]. Adam Rousseau of the Fiat Group, speaking on Partners MGU, reads surprise billing rules as a huge opportunity rather than the end of RBP and sees RBP eventually becoming an RBP network built on direct contracting, while host Vince Lewis reports a producer forced back to a conventional PPO within months [YEFRBSmT3IE @ 00:03:08]. One camp bets on pure network replacement; the other wants a network to fall back on.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The fastest reversal on record is a full unwind. Vince Lewis at Partners MGU took a call from a producer whose January RBP client had to convert back to a conventional PPO just a few months in, because employees kept complaining about balance bills from the local provider and requests for cash upfront before treatment; Lewis calls it a morale issue at best and a public relations nightmare in the media [YEFRBSmT3IE @ 00:00:29]. Arif traces the stigma to early vendors that ended up in litigious fights with hospitals or acted as repricers that slammed a plan in to make a sale with no advocacy or education, and admits deals have gone sideways on ClaimDOC groups too when the team could not get access to HR and rank-and-file employees [mPaz9R2yMrs @ 00:08:26]. Micro-Dyn spells out the mechanism: when providers reject the benchmark rate, the patient can receive a balance bill for the difference [Hz5wBrKavxY @ 00:01:14]. Deihl adds the collections trap, where billing companies historically dinged credit right away and sent accounts straight to collections, so the carriers The General Agency works with mail hold letters to providers while a claim is under negotiation [FPcS3pupwwA @ 00:07:38].

Access friction is the second bottleneck, and it is measurable. Arif estimates about 85% of outpatient facility claims flow through with no problems before care, leaving roughly 15% with friction; eight or nine of every ten of those get worked out, which leaves one to two percent of procedures where the surgery slips a week or the doctor has to move it to another facility. The nightmare version is a provider calling at 7 p.m. Central to secure a contract for an 8 a.m. surgery the next day [mPaz9R2yMrs @ 00:22:14]. In markets controlled by one dominant system, often rural, ClaimDOC contracts with as many freestanding ambulatory surgery centers as possible and leans on the Consolidated Appropriations Act for emergency rooms, which cannot balance bill the member or turn care away, a fallback the provider relations team calls plan B [A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:38:56]. Benefits Studio flags the same catch: some hospitals refuse to take part, which can leave gaps in access [noY8cLblMi4 @ 00:01:49]. Bricker warns that direct contracts stall without navigation, because employees end up getting lost, and notes that getting a major ASO to administer one has been super hard, so independent TPAs build client specific networks instead [xcu6bvj22fc @ 00:04:03].

The economics checks start with the bill itself. Arif describes hospitals unbundling ICU charges that are supposed to be an all-in per diem, billing oxygen, ventilator, ECMO, and even nursing separately on COVID stays, so claims that should have been billed at a fraction of that came in at $23 million and tripped an outlier clause that turned a supposed 50% PPO discount into 15% [mPaz9R2yMrs @ 00:35:10]. Micro-Dyn warns that under RBP coding errors can multiply into bigger financial losses than under contract pricing [Hz5wBrKavxY @ 00:01:34]. Deihl keeps quotes honest: a demographically older 29-employee group priced at $334 per employee on RBP against $678 on the PPO, booked as 202% savings, but most of the time the agency sees anywhere from 15% to 70%, and these plans are medically underwritten [FPcS3pupwwA @ 00:04:56]. Stein calls the EOB headline a trap of its own, where a hospital bills $96,000, the administrator touts a $40,000 discount, and the chargemaster number was never what anyone expected to collect, an opacity that benefits every party except self-funded plans [D3AuT-Ki3nw @ 00:06:10]. Measure cost per employee per month and real dollars paid, not discount percentages.

callout.title: Kill-Switch Checks Before Pulling the Network Off the ID Card
callout.body: Every one of these gates maps to a failure an operator lived through: a PPO unwind, a slam-in rollout that went sideways, a dominant system shutting the door, or fees quietly eating the spread. Clear all four before the effective date.
items: Lock in access to HR and rank-and-file employees for education before go-live, because deals without that access went sideways [Dysrupt Healthcare Podcast — mPaz9R2yMrs @ 00:08:26].
Map dominant-system and rural markets and contract freestanding ambulatory surgery centers as plan B before members need surgery [Self-Funded — A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:38:56].
Stand up balance-bill advocates before employees face cash-upfront demands, the complaints that forced one client back to a conventional PPO within months [Partners MGU — YEFRBSmT3IE @ 00:00:29].
Get TPA and repricing fees quoted and net them against projected savings, since repricing fees can eat into the saving [Benefits Studio — noY8cLblMi4 @ 00:01:12].

Pull a top-utilization report and let members nominate their doctors during open enrollment so the vendor can call each provider before the first claim [Self-Funded — A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:27:31].

Put the implementation team in place two to three months before the effective date to run open enrollment communication, and keep the drip running all plan year [Self-Funded — A__ZFq9k8Ds @ 00:41:13].
