chapters.question_prompt: What should an employer expect from a benefits broker, how are brokers paid, and how does a broker of record letter move an account?
chapters.title: Brokers, Commissions, and the Broker of Record Letter
chapters.subtitle: Broker value and selection criteria, commissions including MEC plans, when to fire your broker, building a competitive benefits program, and BOR letter mechanics and myths across benefits and P&C lines
chapters.executive_summary: Benefits and commercial brokers agree the employer pays its broker through commission built into the premium, around 5% or 3 to 6% of premium, and that percentage pay rises with every renewal while persistency bonuses reward clients staying put. Benefits Blake cites a $178 median per enrolled person per year and about $30 more commission per $1,000 of extra premium, then shows how to force disclosure of direct and indirect pay of $1,000 or more and pull Form 5500 Schedule A filings for free. Evolved Benefits pitches MEC commissions of 12 to 25%. On broker of record letters, practitioners agree a BOR fires the incumbent, takes five to ten business days, and gives the incumbent a rescind window, but split on whether commission or flat-fee models and free due diligence or paid proposals best align broker and client.

key_metrics.label: Standard Benefits Broker Commission
key_metrics.context: Most common commission structure on employer health plans, paid back to the broker through the insurance carrier and embedded in the monthly premium.

key_metrics.label: Median Fully Insured Broker Commission
key_metrics.value: $178 per enrolled person per year (about $15 a month)
key_metrics.context: Johns Hopkins study of Form 5500 filings on almost 30,000 fully insured health plans covering about 11 million employees, built on 2017 filings.

key_metrics.label: Commission Rise per Premium Increase
key_metrics.value: About $30 more commission for every $1,000 more premium
key_metrics.context: Same study measured commissions rising with premiums, with the effect strongest on the smallest plans; reported as a correlation, not proof of causation.

key_metrics.label: MEC Plan Commission Window
key_metrics.context: MEC plan commissions offered versus roughly 5% on major medical, varying by group size, wage ordinance areas, and supplemental products.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus: Who Pays the Broker and What the BOR Actually Does
paragraphs: The benefits practitioners start from the same blunt fact: the employer is already paying the broker, it just never sees the invoice. Benefits Blake splits broker pay into two buckets, direct commission that is 'bundled right into your rate' and indirect money the carrier pays the agency, and says most employers have no idea what they pay because 'you just don't see the line item' [m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:01:56]. Benefits On The Fly says the same thing from 25 years of selling: most owners have 'absolutely no idea how much their broker is actually making,' and the dominant model is commission rather than fee [50kdf1lBaO8 @ 00:00:31]. Butch Zemar adds the mechanical reason clients treat brokers as a free commodity: premiums are filed with the state with commissions already incorporated, so they are built in whether or not an agent is used [2DrBScDIwrk @ 00:00:42]. Rodney Mattos frames the fully insured buyer's position as 'one premium, one lever, one renewal conversation,' with the advisor's pay sitting inside the same bill as carrier administration and profit [bmIls2hM4uk @ 00:01:11]. The baseline prerequisite all four share: before judging whether a broker is worth it, convert the hidden commission into a dollar figure you can actually argue about.

The second point of agreement is that percentage pay rewards the broker when the client loses. Rodney Mattos, who sat at carrier golf outings and incentive dinners early in their career as a producer, says the unspoken rule was 'keep the client happy, keep the premiums flowing,' and that a 10% premium jump lifts a percentage commission 10% with 'no extra effort required' [bmIls2hM4uk @ 00:02:59]. Benefits On The Fly admits the same discomfort from inside the commission model: they could justify their 5% with HR support and claims advocacy, yet 'I still kept making more money every time my client was hit with a premium increase' [50kdf1lBaO8 @ 00:03:55]. Benefits Blake isolates the sharpest lever, persistency compensation, which pays the agency more 'when clients stay put. Not when they do better' [m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:06:46]. Butch Zemar confirms that at the top end, enough volume unlocks retention bonuses that create 'a financial incentive for the insurance broker to not shop plans,' though they say those land at big shops, not small and mid-sized agencies [2DrBScDIwrk @ 00:02:50]. None of these speakers call the industry crooked; Blake's line is that you do not need conscious bad intent for an incentive to work against somebody, you just need the wrong incentive to exist year after year.

On the broker of record letter, the property, casualty, aviation and malpractice brokers converge on identical mechanics. Beyond Business Insurance defines it as a letter that 'essentially fires your current agent and hires another agent': the client signs it on letterhead, it goes to the carrier, and in usually five to ten business days the new agent is assigned, because carriers work with only one agent at a time [rnj58CEkGiE @ 00:00:48]. BWI Aviation Insurance's Matt White, who has watched hundreds of these letters over 11 years, says the carrier then gives the current broker five business days to obtain a rescinding letter before the policy transfers [LDwFFXhIu_U @ 00:01:19]. Strategic Builders-Dev calls that window 'the tick tock': the current agent gets five days to hold the request and call the client to rescind, so expect an uncomfortable call [79EPdRvCp3A @ 00:01:50]. eQuoteMD's Tim Ryan puts it at five to ten days and adds that the letter only applies to the specific carrier named, not to any other company in the market [IeLvLNXVKEo @ 00:03:18]. The shared rule: sign a BOR only to fire the incumbent or change who holds access to a market, never as a casual favor to get a quote.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The commission math is simple enough to run on a napkin, and the practitioners want owners to run it themselves. Benefits On The Fly's formula: take the monthly premium check, multiply by 5%, then by 12. Their worked case is 50 enrolled employees at $500 a month, a $25,000 monthly check or $300,000 a year, with $1,250 a month flowing back to the broker through the carrier [50kdf1lBaO8 @ 00:01:29]. Rodney Mattos uses the 3 to 6% base commission range ProPublica reported in 2019: on a $1 million plan that is $30,000 to $60,000 a year, and a 10% premium increase lifts it 10% [bmIls2hM4uk @ 00:02:59]. Benefits Blake scales it to a 250-life fully insured group paying $2 million at 5%, a $100,000 commission; a 10% renewal pushes premium to $2.2 million and the broker to $110,000, so the employer eats a $200,000 problem while the advisor collects a $10,000 raise for less work [m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:08:03]. Blake then shows why self-funding can cut the broker's pay: the premium base collapses to stop-loss premium and admin fees because claims money stays in the employer's account, so the honest recommendation and the profitable one point in opposite directions [m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:09:35].

The second toolset is disclosure plus public filings. Benefits Blake says that under the Consolidated Appropriations Act, brokers on ERISA group health plans are covered service providers under Section 408(b)(2) and must disclose in writing any direct or indirect compensation of $1,000 or more, reasonably in advance of signing, renewing, or extending, for any contract since December 27, 2021 [m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:11:22]. Blake's ask: named dollar figures, not 'commissions vary,' and the last three years if you have never seen one. Enforcement is soft, with no filing and no penalty schedule, but a missing disclosure makes the contract unreasonable and creates prohibited transaction exposure. The free side-channel is the Form 5500 Schedule A, which reports commissions and fees paid to agents and brokers; Blake pulls it on the EFAST2 search site in about two minutes and points out every other employer's filing is public too, so you can benchmark peers your size in your area [m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:15:54]. The catch: Schedule A runs about a plan year behind and misses agency-level indirect money, so treat it as the floor, not the ceiling [m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:17:00]. Rodney Mattos adds the one question to put to any advisor, themselves included: how does your pay change if we stay, if we cut, or if we switch [bmIls2hM4uk @ 00:06:27].

On the commercial side, Max Revenue's Micah lays out how a producer earns a BOR without asking a stranger to sign anything on day one. The sequence: build rapport, ask why the prospect took the meeting, have them rate their insurance experience on a 1-to-10 scale and say what would make it a 10, ask when they last went to market, then give a 30-second to one-minute explanation that underwriters release one quote to one agent per year, so whoever arrives first blocks everyone else [vTPBeVqiUY4 @ 00:17:48]. The pivot is the house-sale analogy: competitors scrap multi-agent quoting and hire the one agent who will market and stage them best, an approach Micah says has saved their clients an average of 17% [vTPBeVqiUY4 @ 00:22:14]. The ask is a no-cost review of premiums, coverages, and a marketing plan that does not tip off the incumbent, and Micah is upfront that about 70% of the time it simply confirms the client is in a good spot [vTPBeVqiUY4 @ 00:24:01]. Butch Zemar describes the paid version for benefits: charge for the proposal, credit it back if the broker wins the business, and write in performance-based wording so a broker who does not perform does not get paid [2DrBScDIwrk @ 00:21:58].

callout.title: How Practitioners Pressure-Test a Broker Before Firing One
callout.body: These are the moves brokers themselves use to expose what a broker earns and to keep a BOR from blowing up mid-switch.
items: Request the 408(b)(2) compensation statement in named dollar figures and watch the response: a confident broker sends it the same week, while stalling, defensiveness, or a summary instead of figures tells you something [Benefits Blake — m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:19:46].

Pull a few Form 5500 filings from companies your size in your area on EFAST2; every employer's Schedule A is public, so you can see what peers pay their brokers [Benefits Blake — m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:16:12].

Never sign a BOR because an agent claims it is needed to get quotes; you do not need to sign anything but applications, and only sign to fire the incumbent or move market access [Beyond Business Insurance — rnj58CEkGiE @ 00:02:47].

Expect the incumbent to call within the five-day hold window asking you to rescind, and be ready to either ignore the call or have the difficult conversation [Strategic Builders-Dev Insurance & Risk Solutions — 79EPdRvCp3A @ 00:01:50].

sop_steps.title: Price the Current Broker in Dollars
sop_steps.action: Convert the embedded commission into a monthly and annual figure.
sop_steps.detail: Multiply the monthly premium check by 5% and then by 12; on 50 employees at $500 a month that is a $25,000 check and $1,250 a month to the broker [Benefits On The Fly — 50kdf1lBaO8 @ 00:01:45].

sop_steps.title: Force Disclosure and Pull Schedule A
sop_steps.action: Request the 408(b)(2) statement and download your own Form 5500 Schedule A before the next renewal meeting.
sop_steps.detail: Ask for named direct and indirect figures, plus the last three years if never received; take two minutes to pull the 5500 and five minutes to read Schedule A, then watch how the request gets handled [Benefits Blake — m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:19:26].

sop_steps.title: Run Due Diligence Before Any BOR
sop_steps.action: Have the challenger review premiums, coverages, and a marketing plan without tipping off the incumbent.
sop_steps.detail: The review answers whether you are overpaying, overexposed, and how to look more attractive to underwriters, with no time suck and no ruffled feathers with the current agent [Max Revenue — vTPBeVqiUY4 @ 00:23:23].

sop_steps.title: Execute the BOR With Eyes Open
sop_steps.action: Confirm the carrier's BOR rules, sign on letterhead, and plan for the transition period.
sop_steps.detail: Some carriers refuse midterm BORs or any BOR at all [Rob Freeman | Insuring The Built Environment — C_YjzkmKog0 @ 00:01:17]; the outgoing agent keeps commission through the end of that year while the new agent effectively works for free until the new policy [Beyond Business Insurance — rnj58CEkGiE @ 00:03:34].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over how the advisor should get paid. Benefits On The Fly ran the standard 5% commission play for years, showing prospects they were already paying their broker and listing HR support, automated onboarding, compliance and claims advocacy to justify the check, then abandoned it because every premium increase raised their own income: 'I was winning while my client was losing' [50kdf1lBaO8 @ 00:03:55]. Their replacement is a flat fee billed directly to the client, with every commission, bonus and incentive disclosed. rodneymattos frames the same fault line: base commissions of 3 to 6% rise in lockstep with premium, while the per-employee flat fee many advisors now charge does not grow with your rate [bmIls2hM4uk @ 00:02:59]. Butch Zemar pushes from the other side. On a 10-life group the agency collects roughly $3,600 a year, but proposal, enrollment and service work priced at $300 an hour totals about $3,900, so the broker is in the hole before technology, HR help or wellness programs are counted [2DrBScDIwrk @ 00:15:29]. Their fix is a hybrid: charge for the proposal, credit it back against fees or commissions on a win, and write performance-based language so a broker who does not deliver gives up pay [2DrBScDIwrk @ 00:22:13].

Practitioners also split on whether commission keeps a broker carrier-neutral. Lee Soo, a licensed broker interviewed on The HR Hub, argues group commissions are pretty standard across carriers, so the broker gets paid wherever the business lands, while a carrier selling direct only pushes its own plan; they concede volume bonuses exist for brokers with a lot of business at one carrier [d5PvJwohdPU @ 00:02:43]. Benefits Blake says neutrality breaks at the agency level: overrides, growth bonuses and persistency bonuses pay more when clients simply stay, and moving a sound group to self-funding collapses the premium base and can cut the broker's pay [m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:09:35]. Butch Zemar places retention bonuses with the big shops, saying they create a financial incentive not to shop plans, while small and mid-size agencies collect level commissions [2DrBScDIwrk @ 00:02:50]. Evolved Benefits runs a different playbook altogether: MEC plans pay 12 to upwards of 25% monthly versus about 5% on major medical, and on a 200-employee group with only 8 or 9 on major medical, MEC enrollment of 50 to 80 lands commissions on par with or above the major medical check [H0MJJJNfYdo @ 00:02:23]. They pitch it as covering employees who could never afford even the leanest bronze plan.

The broker of record letter splits practitioners into camps. Beyond Business Insurance calls it a great tool with three legitimate uses: firing your agent, letting a new agent into a carrier your current agent already blocked, or letting your current agent reclaim a market a shopper reached first, and insists you never need to sign anything just to get quotes [rnj58CEkGiE @ 00:02:47]. BWI Aviation Insurance is stricter, calling 'sign this BOR and I can get you a better rate' the worst and most misleading way to use the letter [LDwFFXhIu_U @ 00:00:16]. Strategic Builders-Dev only requests a BOR when the prospect says they are unhappy with their agent, and tells a well-placed client to stay where they are [79EPdRvCp3A @ 00:00:40]. Max Revenue skips the letter as an opener entirely. Micah pitches free due diligence on premiums, coverages and underwriter feedback, a review agencies have billed at $5,000 to $15,000, then frames the decision like hiring one real estate agent to sell a house; they claim an average 17% savings and admit roughly 70% of reviews simply confirm the client is in a good spot [vTPBeVqiUY4 @ 00:24:01]. Their own label for the method is plain due diligence dressed up under the BOR name.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap is invisible math. Benefits Blake runs it on a 250-life group paying $2 million a year at 5% commission: $100,000 to the broker. A 10% renewal lifts premium to $2.2 million and the broker's check to $110,000, so the employer inherits a $200,000 problem while the advisor collects a $10,000 raise for less work, because accepting a renewal is easier than changing carriers [m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:08:03]. rodneymattos shows the same shape inside the medical loss ratio: on a $1 million plan up to $150,000 can go to everything besides care, and a 10% increase lifts that allowance to $165,000 [bmIls2hM4uk @ 00:01:57]. They also report carrier bonuses of up to $150,000 for a single group, some tied to keeping the employer with that carrier at renewal rather than lowering cost, and admit sitting through the carrier golf outings and incentive dinners as a young producer [bmIls2hM4uk @ 00:03:16]. Benefits On The Fly flags the behavioral tell: a broker you rarely hear from all year who pops up only at renewal, to make sure you renew so they keep getting paid, is a sign to start shopping for a different broker [50kdf1lBaO8 @ 00:02:02].

The second trap is assuming disclosure law protects you. Benefits Blake notes that brokers expecting $1,000 or more in direct or indirect compensation must disclose it in writing ahead of a renewal, yet enforcement is thin: a 2021 field assistance bulletin, no filing, no penalty schedule, only prohibited transaction exposure if the disclosure never happened [m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:12:51]. The reasonableness call belongs to the CFO who signs off, not the broker, so an employer who never received the statement is sitting on an unmet fiduciary obligation [m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:15:17]. Blake also cools the lawsuit hype: four December 2025 class actions named brokers beside LabCorp, Community Health Systems, United Airlines and Allied Universal over voluntary benefit commissions of 22 to 40%, but the Johnson and Johnson and Wells Fargo health plan cases were each dismissed on standing twice. Benefits On The Fly turned full commission and bonus accounting into a selling point, pitching it as keeping clients compliant with their CAA fiduciary requirements [50kdf1lBaO8 @ 00:05:24]. rodneymattos adds the reading discipline: the disclosure should land with whoever is responsible for the plan before you sign, and you read the bonuses, not just the commission [bmIls2hM4uk @ 00:05:56].

BOR execution carries its own landmines. BWI Aviation Insurance warns that when a second broker gets you to sign a BOR to unlock carriers the first broker already approached, the second broker takes over every quote the first broker worked up, and these letters tend to create more issues than they solve [LDwFFXhIu_U @ 00:02:04]. Their rule of thumb: research reviews beforehand, pick one great broker, and let only that broker shop the market. Rob Freeman warns that some carriers refuse midterm BORs and some refuse BORs entirely, so owning the choice of broker does not guarantee the carrier will honor a switch [C_YjzkmKog0 @ 00:01:37]. Beyond Business Insurance spells out the economics: the outgoing agent keeps commission through the end of that year, while the new agent is essentially working for free until the new policy takes effect [rnj58CEkGiE @ 00:03:47]. On the selling side, Butch Zemar describes employers who collect one broker's research and proposal, then hand it to their current broker to execute, which is why they now charge for the proposal and credit it back if they win the business [2DrBScDIwrk @ 00:21:32]. Their line to employers: you can take the proposal, they just need to get paid for that time.

callout.title: Kill Switches Before You Sign, Switch, or Self-Fund
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, reversal, or bottleneck practitioners reported firsthand. Clear all four before a renewal signature, a BOR, or a funding change.
items: Demand the written compensation disclosure with named dollar figures for direct and indirect pay; a broker who stalls, gets defensive, or sends a summary instead of figures has told you something [Benefits Blake — m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:20:01].
Never sign a BOR just to get quotes; sign only to fire your current agent or to change who has access to a specific market [Beyond Business Insurance — rnj58CEkGiE @ 00:03:02].

Confirm the carrier accepts midterm BORs at all, and budget for the five-to-ten day window the incumbent gets to talk you into rescinding [Rob Freeman | Insuring The Built Environment — C_YjzkmKog0 @ 00:01:37] [eQuoteMD — IeLvLNXVKEo @ 00:02:12].

Hold off on self-funding if cash flow cannot take a swing or nobody on the team will look at the data; the 85% floor and rebate disappear while administrator, PBM, stop loss and advisor fees remain [rodneymattos — bmIls2hM4uk @ 00:06:58].

chapters.pull_quote: 'There's literally a line item in this industry that pays your advisor for you not to change carriers.' — Benefits Blake (m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:06:46).
action_checklist: Request the 408(b)(2) compensation statement from your broker with named dollar figures for direct and indirect pay, and ask for the last three years if you never received it [Benefits Blake — m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:19:09].

Pull your own Form 5500 Schedule A on EFAST2, then pull filings from similar-sized employers in your area to benchmark broker commissions, treating the number as a floor [Benefits Blake — m68BBrL5G18 @ 00:16:12].
Multiply your monthly premium by 5% and then by 12 to see roughly what a commission broker earns on your plan each year [Benefits On The Fly — 50kdf1lBaO8 @ 00:01:01].
Ask your advisor exactly how their pay changes if you stay, cut, or switch, and request your own cost and claims information in writing [rodneymattos — bmIls2hM4uk @ 00:06:27].
Before signing a BOR, confirm it applies only to the specific carrier named and that you are ready to lose the old broker, since it removes them from the policy [eQuoteMD — IeLvLNXVKEo @ 00:03:18].

Producers: run the due diligence meeting in order, building rapport, asking why they took the meeting, explaining how carriers block markets, then presenting the one-broker alternative [Max Revenue — vTPBeVqiUY4 @ 00:30:48].

chapters.question_prompt: What does the Consolidated Appropriations Act require of health plan sponsors, and how do disclosure and filing duties turn into leverage over vendors?
chapters.title: CAA Compliance: Gag Clauses, Disclosures, and Plan Filings
chapters.subtitle: Gag clause bans and attestations, broker and consultant compensation disclosures, transparency provisions, new fiduciary obligations, contract review, and Form 5500 filing and late-filing penalty relief
chapters.executive_summary: Benefits lawyers, brokers and compliance shops converge on one message: the CAA makes every ERISA health plan sponsor, fully insured groups included, a fiduciary who can delegate tasks but never liability. The street playbook is to strip gag clauses from carrier, ASO and PBM contracts, attest every year, force brokers and consultants expecting more than $1,000 to disclose direct and indirect compensation in dollars and cents, and terminate holdouts within 90 days after a missed 30-day disclosure window. The numbers set the stakes: $100 per day per employee in penalties, a Florida school system that expected about $195,000 in provider pay and found roughly $4 million, and DFVCP cutting late Form 5500 penalties from $2,739 to $10 a day. Practitioners split on the attestation date (December 27 versus December 31), on the bill's length (1,100 versus 6,000 pages), and on whether vendor payments can ever lower a sponsor's fees.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator on this beat starts from one premise: the employer is the fiduciary, and that status sticks whether anyone signs up for it or not. Tony Sorrentino of HPFID, a CPA and attorney who coaches brokers through the rollout, puts it bluntly: "delegate responsibility you can never delegate liability if you don't do this it's on you" [I7g6idLkgrc @ 00:29:13]. Benefits lawyer Michael Flanagan goes further, warning that a person does not even need to be aware they are a fiduciary to carry the exposure, because functional fiduciaries are created by what they do, not by what the paperwork says, and a claims administrator stays a fiduciary even when its contract disclaims the role [9hPiS9wv_F4 @ 00:07:55]. Jamie Greenleaf of OneVision tells sponsors that at the end of the day they are the fiduciary unless their vendors are signing off that they are fiduciaries, and the liabilities lie with the sponsor [ks-F1VjDtk4 @ 00:18:05]. Jason Andrade of the Mahoney Group lands the line that resets small-group conversations: fully insured employers are now fiduciaries too, so sitting behind a carrier policy is no longer a hiding place [l5tGs_zQ8xA @ 00:04:02]. The working baseline is identical across all four voices: name the fiduciaries, run a documented decision process, and assume every gap in vendor oversight lands on the sponsor's own balance sheet rather than on the vendor that caused it.

The second point of agreement is that gag clauses are dead and the sponsor has to prove it every year. Chad Burdo of HUB Midwest East explains the old play: insurers and PBMs restricted what pharmacists could tell members, so a member could be bound to a $15 negotiated rate when a cheaper option existed; now plans must review insurer and PBM contracts and "attest every single year by December 31st" that those contracts are compliant [JY_hbh9Kxrc @ 00:01:42]. Julia of Berger Montague takes the fight upstream into self-insured ASO agreements, where gag language blocks the employer from its own claims and price data and therefore from its duty to monitor and confirm that costs are reasonable [WBl8smrz_3E @ 00:00:53]. Clear Value Benefit Compliance adds that contracts with providers, networks or TPAs cannot block de-identified claims access, provider quality data, or sharing with business associates, with attestations due by December 31 of each year going forward [wEKxSVkV2NA @ 00:01:20]. Mel DeWeese tells employers directly that they carry a new stated fiduciary responsibility to vet that those clauses have actually been removed from their health insurance plans [k0FZkQKH4SQ @ 00:07:35]. Nobody in this group treats the attestation as optional paperwork; it is the annual receipt proving the sponsor's data pipe is open and being watched.

Third, the practitioners agree the CAA ports the retirement-plan fee playbook straight into health benefits. Karen of Berger Montague ties it to 408(b)(2): fiduciaries were "asleep at the switch" on healthcare fees, and the new broker and consultant rules mirror the 401k regime that let sponsors judge whether service agreements were reasonable and avoid prohibited transactions [3ZIAPoIvjvc @ 00:00:41]. Mark Fisher of Advanced Benefits states the trigger plainly: the disclosure and transparency rules hit all ERISA plans that pay any party more than a thousand dollars a year [twKQWqVJ4zc @ 00:00:32]. The Leapfrog Group panel uses the same $1,000 line for expected direct or indirect compensation and applies it to brokers and consultants alike, which puts every renewal relationship under the microscope [QU7rxyEAEjQ @ 00:10:51]. On enforcement, the shared fear is plaintiffs rather than Washington. Jason Andrade concedes regulators "certainly could be" breathing down a sponsor's neck, but rates participant lawsuits as the more likely hit, and frames the upside as finally seeing exactly what the plan pays for and which brokers deliver the best value for their fees [sIp9x3Y9ePw @ 00:00:33]. The common conclusion is that the same disclosures that create exposure also hand a sharp sponsor the leverage to renegotiate, rebid, or fire an overpaid intermediary.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The gag-clause workflow the Berger Montague panel teaches is sequenced and unforgiving. Rule one: "you can't extend any contract with someone who won't remove the get clause" [WBl8smrz_3E @ 00:01:38]. If a sponsor is stuck mid-contract with a holdout, Julia's sequence is to document the refusal in writing, tell the DOL, and then escalate: the employer "might need to file a lawsuit" either to get the information it is entitled to or to terminate the contract for breach and seek damages [WBl8smrz_3E @ 00:02:12]. The annual attestation then explains any clause that could not be removed, and the panel's tone is that this is not optional: you better do it, and do it now. Karen pushes past the paperwork into the money: once the data flows, audit the claims, because claims data surfaces what no disclosure will, such as somebody being paid twice for an operation on the same day for the same person, cross-plan offsetting, and improper claim reductions [WBl8smrz_3E @ 00:03:01]. On the review step itself, the Miller Johnson team tells sponsors to read the carrier and ASA agreements and request an attestation from the TPA or carrier rather than relying on assumptions about who handled it [WVU2CeENchc @ 00:24:42]. The operating logic is simple: no data access, no renewal, and a written record of every refusal.

The broker-compensation mechanics come with hard clocks. The Leapfrog Group panel spells out the escalation: if a covered service provider does not deliver the disclosure "within 30 days," the sponsor has to notify the Department of Labor and then terminate the contract within 90 days [QU7rxyEAEjQ @ 00:11:35]. Galpin flags the indirect money hiding in plain sight: an insurer advertising bonuses of up to $150,000 per employer group, and brokers being offered Hawaii trips for placing business [QU7rxyEAEjQ @ 00:29:17]. Mark Fisher of Advanced Benefits warns that brokers may be earning fees on every single pharmacy script, and that certain large brokerage firms run coalitions that hide these fees, so even simple plans pay brokers thousands of dollars the employer never sees; the question that matters is what services those dollars actually buy [twKQWqVJ4zc @ 00:00:50]. The OneVision case study shows the scale of the leak: a Florida school system expected about $195,000 in service-provider compensation and found roughly $4 million over four years once the numbers were surfaced [ks-F1VjDtk4 @ 00:17:25]. Practitioners treat the disclosure request as the opening move of a fee audit, not a formality, and push sponsors to compare every dollar against the services delivered before signing any renewal or extension.

The filing side runs on two engines: RxDC reporting and Form 5500. Mel DeWeese walks the RxDC build file by file: a P-file carrying plan name and number, plan year dates, members as of December 31, and the issuer, TPA and PBM names and EINs, then D-files D1 through D8 covering premium and life-years, spending by category, the top 50 most frequent brand drugs, the top 50 most costly drugs, the top 50 by spending increase, Rx totals, rebates by therapeutic class, and rebates on the top 25 drugs, plus a response narrative [k0FZkQKH4SQ @ 00:09:29]. For D1 life-years, the working shortcut is to "add all 12 numbers together and then divide by 12" [k0FZkQKH4SQ @ 00:11:19]. Foundation Benefits flags the 5500 gotcha that catches mid-size groups: a 125 to 150 employee shop may have only 75 to 80 on medical, but an employer-paid LTD or basic life plan with 110 enrolled still triggers the filing [R-MOuJrCG9Q @ 00:01:00]. When a filing is missed, HR Service, Inc. runs the DFVCP math: $2,739 per day per plan outside the program versus $10 per day inside it, capped at $1,500 for small plans and $4,000 for large plans [K_Kmaqdjrns @ 00:09:00]. That spread is the entire case for self-reporting fast.

Brokers use the per-day figure to open compliance conversations with larger employers

callout.title: Small Moves That Change the Penalty and Fee Math
callout.body: Operators shared these practical edges for cutting exposure and spotting hidden compensation.
items: Wrap multiple welfare benefits into one plan with an SPD wrap so a single $4,000 DFVCP cap applies instead of one cap per plan [HR Service, Inc. — K_Kmaqdjrns @ 00:09:47]
Penalties start accumulating the day after the original due date, not after the extension due date, so a late 5558 buys nothing [HR Service, Inc. — K_Kmaqdjrns @ 00:10:11]
If a broker says the compensation information is already on the 5500, the sponsor is being gaslit; demand the CAA disclosure itself [The Leapfrog Group — QU7rxyEAEjQ @ 00:56:32]

For brokers selling compliance services, one won 50-life group pays for the compliance cost, which is why it is framed as 10 percent compliance and 90 percent opportunity [Self-Funded — I7g6idLkgrc @ 00:41:08]

sop_steps.title: Charter the Fiduciary Committee
sop_steps.action: Seat the CFO, CEO, COO and HR on a conflict-free committee, adopt a charter, and keep minutes of every decision.
sop_steps.detail: Greenleaf's action plan pairs the committee with fiduciary training, a charter and data gathering [OneVision — ks-F1VjDtk4 @ 00:19:07]; Flanagan's list is identify fiduciaries, hold meetings with minutes, get fiduciary education, and review the process [Walsh Insurance — 9hPiS9wv_F4 @ 00:16:47].

sop_steps.title: Scrub Every Contract for Gag Language
sop_steps.action: Pull insurer, PBM, TPA and ASO agreements, flag gag clauses, and refuse to extend with any holdout.
sop_steps.detail: Burdo's workflow starts with reviewing insurer and PBM contracts before attesting [HUB Midwest East (fka Henriott) — JY_hbh9Kxrc @ 00:01:20]; the Berger Montague panel bars extending any contract with a vendor who will not remove the clause [Berger Montague — WBl8smrz_3E @ 00:01:38].

sop_steps.title: Force Dollar-Level Compensation Disclosures
sop_steps.action: Request written broker and consultant disclosures in dollars, judge reasonableness, then document the finding or rebid.
sop_steps.detail: Sponsors should demand dollars and cents [The Leapfrog Group — QU7rxyEAEjQ @ 00:14:18]; if expenses are unreasonable, issue an RFP and a termination notice, and if reasonable, document that finding [The Leapfrog Group — QU7rxyEAEjQ @ 00:12:13].

sop_steps.title: Calendar Every Filing and Attestation
sop_steps.action: Lock the gag-clause attestation, RxDC P-file and D-files, and Form 5500 deadlines into one compliance calendar with an assigned filer.
sop_steps.detail: Attestations are due by December 31 each year [Clear Value Benefit Compliance — wEKxSVkV2NA @ 00:01:20]; RxDC requires the P-file plus D1 through D8 [Mel 😊 DeWeese — k0FZkQKH4SQ @ 00:09:29]; Form 5500 is due 7 months after plan year end with Form 5558 adding 2.5 months [HR Service, Inc. — K_Kmaqdjrns @ 00:03:47].

sections.heading: 3. Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The calendar itself is contested ground. Tony Sorrentino of HPFID, a CPA and attorney, dates the CAA to December 27, 2020 and tells brokers the gag-clause attestation covers every ERISA plan down to two lives, due December 27, 2022, with under 5% of brokers ready and the filing looking backward over 2020 to 2021 data [I7g6idLkgrc @ 00:28:09]. Chad Burdo at HUB Midwest East runs a different clock: review insurer and PBM contracts, then attest every single year by December 31st that those contracts comply [JY_hbh9Kxrc @ 00:01:42]. Clear Value Benefit Compliance pushes the first attestation out to December 31, 2023, reaching back to December 27, 2020, and pegs every later filing to December 31 of each year [wEKxSVkV2NA @ 00:01:03]. Even the size of the law splits the room. Sorrentino counts roughly 1,100 pages with 91 pages on fiduciary duties, while OneVision co-founder Jamie Greenleaf describes about 6,000 pages with 90 on healthcare [ks-F1VjDtk4 @ 00:00:22]. The operator play is to calendar the earliest date any practitioner names, run the contract review before it, and treat December 31 as the recurring annual drop-dead line rather than betting on a single figure, because an attestation filed late against any of these clocks is still a missed filing.

Where the hammer falls is the second fault line. Sorrentino expects DOL may make an example of a Fortune 50 or 100 company but names participant lawsuits as the bigger fear, and when host Spencer Smith floated the 87,000 new IRS agents as the enforcement engine, Sorrentino's answer was "I really don't know" [I7g6idLkgrc @ 00:39:12]. Jason Andrade of The Mahoney Group concedes regulators from Washington certainly could be breathing down a sponsor's neck, yet ranks plaintiffs' suits as the likelier hit [sIp9x3Y9ePw @ 00:00:33]. On the Ameriflex panel, Andrade splits from Ameriflex counsel on who gets sued: Andrade is skeptical of employer-versus-carrier actions because carriers carry no fiduciary duty, while counsel reports suits surviving the 30- and 60-day marks and emerging within the last six months [l5tGs_zQ8xA @ 00:16:01]. Penalty math diverges too. Sorrentino runs $100 per day per employee, which turns a 1,000-employee group into $100,000 a day, while Greenleaf works the "per belly button" framing on covered lives, so a 300-employee plan with 450 covered members prices out on 450 heads, and still calls class actions the bigger fear [ks-F1VjDtk4 @ 00:23:52]. Model exposure on covered lives, not headcount, and build the paper trail for a plaintiffs' bar before worrying about an audit letter.

When a vendor stonewalls, the playbooks fork. The Leapfrog Group's session lays out a statutory clock: if a broker or consultant does not deliver the disclosure within 30 days, notify the Department of Labor and terminate the contract within 90 days [QU7rxyEAEjQ @ 00:11:35]. Julie on the Berger Montague compensation panel runs a softer front end, requesting the missing disclosure in writing first and reporting to DOL only if the sponsor is still ignored, while assuming every covered service provider must disclose until guidance says otherwise [3ZIAPoIvjvc @ 00:04:14]. On gag-clause holdouts the same firm goes harder: Julia says never extend a contract with a holdout, document the refusal and tell DOL mid-contract, then sue for the data or terminate for breach and seek damages [WBl8smrz_3E @ 00:02:12]. The fee debate is just as split. Galpin at Leapfrog argued vendor payments might lower fees, Thompson shot back that there are no free lunches, yet the same session holds that paying more is not wrong if value is delivered, and Michael Flanagan at Walsh Insurance frames prudence as an evaluation based on value rather than lowest price [9hPiS9wv_F4 @ 00:38:24]. Pick one escalation ladder and write it into the vendor file before the renewal, not after the refusal.

sections.heading: 4. Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The Form 5500 is where groups bleed cash on technicalities. Foundation Benefits flags the classic gotcha: a 125 to 150 employee shop with only 75 to 80 on medical assumes it is under the line, but an employer-paid LTD or basic life plan with 110 enrolled still triggers the filing, and the government penalizes each line separately [R-MOuJrCG9Q @ 00:01:00]. HR Service, Inc. puts the unmitigated number at $2,739 per day per plan, versus $10 a day under DFVCP capped at $1,500 for small plans and $4,000 for large, with an SPD wrap collapsing several plans into one filing so one $4,000 cap applies instead of one per plan [K_Kmaqdjrns @ 00:09:00]. The same team warns that penalties start the day after the original due date, not the extension date, and lists the errors they see: plan-year confusion, counting dependents or COBRA wrong, assuming the broker or TPA files, and lumping health in with the 401k filing [K_Kmaqdjrns @ 00:10:11]. Emparion's retirement-side trap is a cash balance plan plus a solo 401k that together pass $250,000, such as $150,000 plus $110,000, and slip through the cracks when each plan needed its own 5500-EZ [yGr9BaJ2hJ4 @ 00:00:56]. Every one of these is a counting error, not a strategy error.

The money leak most sponsors never see is indirect compensation buried inside vendor contracts. Greenleaf cites a Florida school system that expected roughly $195,000 in service-provider pay; the actual figure ran about $4 million over four years [ks-F1VjDtk4 @ 00:17:25]. At Leapfrog, Galpin described an insurer advertising bonuses of up to $150,000 per employer group and brokers being offered Hawaii trips, and Fogerty found a 64-page Ameriprise disclosure that on page 22 shields representatives from knowing how they are paid [QU7rxyEAEjQ @ 00:29:17]. Mark Fisher at Alliant Idaho warns that brokers may earn a fee on every pharmacy script, that certain large brokerage coalitions hide these fees, and that even simple plans pay brokers thousands of dollars the employer never knew about [twKQWqVJ4zc @ 00:00:50]. Disclosures alone do not close the gap. Karen on the Berger Montague panel says claims data surfaces what paperwork will not: someone paid twice for an operation on the same day for the same person, cross-plan offsetting, and improper claim reductions, none of which a sponsor can monitor without the raw data [WBl8smrz_3E @ 00:03:01]. If the disclosure total looks clean but nobody has pulled claims, the economics check has not happened, and the sponsor is signing off blind.

The quietest trap is assuming someone else holds the liability. Michael Flanagan at Walsh Insurance warns that a person does not even need to know they are a fiduciary to be one, that personal liability attaches, and that a claims administrator is a fiduciary even when its contract disclaims the role [9hPiS9wv_F4 @ 00:07:55]. Sorrentino of HPFID puts it in one line for brokers: you can delegate responsibility but you can never delegate liability, and if the attestation is not done it is on you [I7g6idLkgrc @ 00:29:13]. Miller Johnson adds the contract reality for self-funded plans: the TPA administers, the plan sponsor stays ultimately liable, and the only way to legally shift the financial obligation when it is the TPA's fault is an indemnification clause [WVU2CeENchc @ 00:34:53]. Mel DeWeese reports the RxDC side is already reversing assumptions, with fully insured carriers mailing letters asking employers to file the D1 premium and life-years file themselves, and stresses that it is the employer's fiduciary responsibility to make sure every form gets done [k0FZkQKH4SQ @ 00:03:25]. Read every carrier letter, check every vendor contract for indemnification language, and stop treating the TPA as a liability sponge, because the bill lands on the sponsor.

callout.title: Stop-Points Before You Sign, File, or Attest
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a trap practitioners hit or watched clients hit. Clear all four before renewing a vendor, filing a 5500, or signing the annual gag-clause attestation.
items: Do not enter, extend, or renegotiate any broker or consultant contract until the compensation disclosure is in hand; if it never arrives, request it in writing and report to DOL [Berger Montague — 3ZIAPoIvjvc @ 00:03:59].

Do not accept a broker's answer that the compensation is already on your 5500; Leapfrog's panel calls that being gaslit, so demand the dollar figures directly [The Leapfrog Group — QU7rxyEAEjQ @ 00:56:32].
Do not sign the gag-clause attestation until claims data has actually been pulled and audited for double payments and improper reductions [Berger Montague — WBl8smrz_3E @ 00:03:15].

Do not wait on a late 5500: DFVCP is only open before a DOL notice arrives, an IRS late-filer letter does not disqualify you, and filing is electronic only [HR Service, Inc. — K_Kmaqdjrns @ 00:07:10].

chapters.pull_quote: "Delegate responsibility, you can never delegate liability. If you don't do this, it's on you." — Tony Sorrentino, attributed to Self-Funded (I7g6idLkgrc @ 00:29:13).
action_checklist: Inventory every ERISA plan including employer-paid LTD and basic life, and count enrollment per policy to see whether any single line crosses the 100 threshold that triggers a Form 5500 [Foundation Benefits — R-MOuJrCG9Q @ 00:01:00].

Send written compensation-disclosure requests to every broker and consultant demanding dollars and cents; if nothing arrives in 30 days, notify DOL and terminate within 90 days [The Leapfrog Group — QU7rxyEAEjQ @ 00:11:35].
Review insurer and PBM contracts for gag clauses and attest every year by December 31st that those contracts are compliant [HUB Midwest East (fka Henriott) — JY_hbh9Kxrc @ 00:01:20].
Pull raw claims data and audit it for double payments, cross-plan offsetting, and improper claim reductions that disclosures will not show [Berger Montague — WBl8smrz_3E @ 00:03:01].
Form a conflict-free fiduciary committee of the CFO, CEO, COO, and HR, get fiduciary training, adopt a charter, and gather plan data [OneVision — ks-F1VjDtk4 @ 00:19:07].
If a 5500 is late, file through DFVCP electronically before any DOL notice and consolidate plans under an SPD wrap so one $4,000 cap applies [HR Service, Inc. — K_Kmaqdjrns @ 00:07:10].

chapters.question_prompt: Why are health plan fiduciaries being sued, and how do third-party administrators and claims data fit into managing that exposure?
chapters.title: ERISA Fiduciary Litigation and TPA Claims Administration
chapters.subtitle: The J&J lawsuit, prescription fiduciary rules, pleading standards, tobacco surcharge class actions, ERISA/CAA compliance, the TPA role in claims processing, self-insured reporting, and reading employer claims reports
chapters.executive_summary: Litigators, benefits attorneys and PBM reformers agree that the 401(k) fee-suit playbook is being ported onto self-funded health plans. The Johnson & Johnson complaint is the template: loyalty and prudence claims built on PBM pricing data that CAA disclosures now expose. The street numbers are stark. Teriflunomide cost $81 to acquire, the plan paid $10,239, and Cost Plus sold it for $28.40. Generics are relabeled as specialty to move reimbursement from AWP minus 87 percent to AWP minus 12 percent. Settlements run $8-15M before fees. Operators answer with documented RFPs, liability caps, short lock-ins, item-level data and claimant-level analytics. Practitioners split on how rigid that process must be. Seyfarth's defense bench calls the steps options, says a committee is not required, and rejects pass-through pricing as the legal standard. Compliance advisors push committees, insurance, bonding and attestations.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Health plans are the new fiduciary battlefield, and the people who litigate and defend these cases agree on why. At Seyfarth Shaw, Sam frames the shift bluntly. 401(k) and 403(b) fee suits are roughly 20 years old and that market is saturated. The plaintiffs' bar is now turning to group health plans, armed with data that CAA 2020 disclosures push into the open, and plan sponsors themselves have started suing their own TPAs [EwDJFTGZkoE @ 00:04:12]. Frier Levitt's panel calls the Johnson & Johnson complaint the first case of its kind: employees suing their own employer over PBM mismanagement. The panel draws a straight line back to the retirement-plan fiduciary suits that came before it [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:03:09]. Justin Burgess opens his compliance briefing on the same note. Group health plan litigation is spiking, he says, and fiduciaries have to monitor fees, PBM fees above all, exactly the issue in the J&J suit [Bq89alxy8qQ @ 00:00:01]. Eric Dailey of Multnomah Group supplies the procedural accelerant. ERISA class filing rates are high, and after Northwestern the burden in these fights lies with the defense [_QhwEj0_Hrg @ 00:00:01]. Every camp reads it the same way. The retirement-plan playbook already exists, the disclosure data now exists, and self-funded health plans with large drug spend sit directly in its path.

The legal spine of these claims is equally settled across the speakers. Ben at Seyfarth Shaw anchors health plan exposure in two ERISA duties, exclusive benefit and prudence. Prudence is measured against the prudent-expert rule, not against what a well-meaning amateur running HR might have done [EwDJFTGZkoE @ 00:19:25]. Frier Levitt's panel compresses the same idea into loyalty and prudence. It points operators to paragraph 7 of the roughly 80-page J&J complaint, where the core allegations are concentrated, and treats that paragraph as the map for what plaintiffs will copy next [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:05:01]. Mike Hill of Total Control Health Plans settles the scope question. Self-funded medical, dental and vision plans are ERISA plans. The J&J class action names both the company and its benefits committee over the PBM and the consultant, not just the vendor [FvXAV4cqPRg @ 00:00:24]. John Barl, on The Alliance webinar, ties the duty to cash: fees must be disclosed, and Johnson & Johnson and Wells Fargo have both been sued over health plan fees [2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:24:14]. Taken together, these four speakers treat a self-funded sponsor as a fiduciary over every dollar routed to TPAs, PBMs, brokers and consultants. A plaintiff will ask two questions about that money: did it serve participants, and would a prudent expert have paid it.

The baseline prerequisites are a written paper trail and a funded backstop. Justin Burgess lays out the floor. Form a committee, train it, document how vendors were selected, watch for hidden fees, and bring in ERISA attorneys. Then back the whole structure with fiduciary insurance and bonding [Bq89alxy8qQ @ 00:00:51]. Ben at Seyfarth Shaw agrees on training, delegation, documentation, audits and market checks, but he pushes back on rigid formalism. He tells sponsors the items are options rather than a checklist and that a committee is not required, while warning that these suits look back six years [EwDJFTGZkoE @ 00:57:22]. Barl's contract point is the hardest edge of the consensus. Without a written contract there is no ERISA Section 408(b)(2) exemption, or as he puts it, 'handshake agreements not going to cut it in this situation' [2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:23:16]. On the claims side, Medilink Global describes what a TPA is supposed to deliver once that paperwork exists: provider empanelment, eligibility checks, letters of guarantee, 24x7 support, and end-to-end adjudication and payment [Tvw5ziI8ANo @ 00:01:12]. The sponsor owns the process even when the TPA runs the claims. With a six-year lookback, an undocumented vendor decision made today stays within a plaintiff's reach for years.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The money mechanics start with how PBMs actually get paid. Ben at Seyfarth Shaw walks through the models. Spread pricing means the PBM buys at $10 and sells to the plan at $20. Pass-through pricing adds a per-employee-per-month fee. Then there is rebate retention, plus the less visible cuts from pharmacy ownership and shared-savings arrangements [EwDJFTGZkoE @ 00:27:30]. Frier Levitt's panel names the current profit engine: generics relabeled as specialty drugs. Those drugs are reimbursed at AWP minus 12 percent instead of AWP minus 87 percent on molecules that cost $1 to $3 a pill, and exclusivity is steered to PBM-owned specialty pharmacies [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:09:14]. Mike Hill gives the headline number from the J&J complaint. Teriflunomide carries an average pharmacy acquisition cost of 91 cents per 14-milligram tablet, or $81 for a 90-day supply. The plan paid $10,239, a 12,403% markup [FvXAV4cqPRg @ 00:02:29]. Pramod John benchmarks the same drug at $28.40 through Cost Plus against roughly $10,000 under the plan, a gap of about 300 times [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:24:16]. For an operator, that arithmetic is the audit. When one molecule shows acquisition cost, transparent retail price and plan-paid price that far apart, the plan has the exact fact pattern plaintiffs are now pleading. Generic and specialty definitions in the PBM contract decide which of those three prices the plan ends up paying.

On the vendor side, John Barl on The Alliance webinar gives the most granular procurement script. Send the RFP to three to six vendors and allow about a month for responses. Summarize the responses in a spreadsheet for a benefits committee to review. Review template contracts from the three finalists, score each vendor on a 1-to-10 scale, and write down why the winner was chosen [2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:37:33]. His negotiating benchmarks are specific. Typical liability caps run $50K per error, $1M per claim, or four times the last 12 months of fees, and he treats those as the starting ranges to argue from [2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:38:42]. On term length, he accepts a one-year lock-in followed by 60 to 90 days' termination for convenience, and he calls a five-year lock-in risky [2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:39:37]. Frier Levitt's fiduciary checklist covers the PBM side of the same desk. Send a CAA letter demanding consultant compensation, audit rebates and spread pricing, and review the formulary and MAC pricing [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:44:54]. Each step leaves a dated record: a scored spreadsheet, finalist contract redlines, a compensation letter, an audit report. Together they turn the abstract prudence duty into a file of evidence. That file shows a process, which is what the Seyfarth and Alliance speakers keep returning to as the core of any health plan defense.

The third mechanic is data, and the speakers agree that sponsors work blind without it. Pramod John says PBMs refuse to give plans their own data. That is why his action steps start with getting item-level pricing, then allowing fills at Cost Plus and other pharmacies, hiring a non-conflicted consultant, and exploring transparent models [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:47:45]. Self Insured Reporting sells the plumbing for that work. It offers more than 100 TPA and PBM integrations and loads a plan's data in under a week, so the sponsor is not waiting on a vendor to send reports [Ci7LnsZjk2g @ 00:00:52]. The AHealthcareZ presenter teaches how to read the output. Decide what you want to see first, then look at claimants rather than claims, by quarter or year. 5% of members drive 50% of costs at more than $100K each, and 20% drive 80% at more than $20K, so the intervention sweet spot is the $20K-$100K band [UQkzQUPP8JE @ 00:02:00]. In a 100-employee plan spending $1M, that means five people spend about $500K and fifteen people about $300K. His facility example sets the stakes: one dialysis patient cost $1M a year, equivalent to $10M in sales at a 10% margin [UQkzQUPP8JE @ 00:07:19]. Out-of-network surgery centers are his next target.

callout.title: Leverage points the speakers actually use
callout.body: These four moves separate operators who control their vendors from sponsors who discover the pricing in a complaint.
items: Read your PBM contract's definitions before you read its price guarantees: 'You should be looking at terms like generic drug or brand name drug and what the definitions are.' [Total Control Health Plans — FvXAV4cqPRg @ 00:03:16]

Load every must-have term into the RFP itself, including limitation of liability, indemnification and data access. 'Once the vendor knows that it won the RFP, employers lose a lot of that leverage.' [theallianceorg — 2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:40:26]

Stop negotiating on discount guarantees. The Frier Levitt panel calls them the wrong metric, citing the Anthony Schiavo / 3 Axis Advisors study, and says 'those are the wrong questions to be asking.' [Frier Levitt — jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:54:25]

Classify large claims as ongoing or complete by ICD-10/CPT code, the way stop-loss carriers do. Cancer and surgical complications tend to keep running; ortho and heart-attack claims are mostly complete. [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — UQkzQUPP8JE @ 00:04:10]

sop_steps.title: Pull your own line-level data
sop_steps.action: Demand item-level pricing from the PBM and TPA and load it into an independent reporting platform.
sop_steps.detail: Pramod John says PBMs refuse to give plans their own data, so item-level pricing is the first action step [Frier Levitt — jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:48:19]. Self Insured Reporting connects to more than 100 TPA and PBM integrations and loads data in under a week [Self Insured Reporting — Ci7LnsZjk2g @ 00:00:52].

sop_steps.title: Run a scored, documented RFP
sop_steps.action: Send the RFP to three to six vendors with must-have terms already embedded, then score finalists 1-to-10 in committee.
sop_steps.detail: Allow about a month for responses, summarize them in a spreadsheet, review template contracts from the three finalists, and document why the winner was chosen [theallianceorg — 2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:37:33].

sop_steps.title: Harden the vendor contract
sop_steps.action: Negotiate the insurance, bonding, error reporting, fiduciary status, human review and exit terms before signing.
sop_steps.detail: Require insurance in the millions, bonding, quarterly reporting of errors the vendor could not fix, and US-based staff [theallianceorg — 2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:50:10]. Have the contract state that a vendor hearing final internal appeals is a fiduciary [theallianceorg — 2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:47:25]. Add post-termination cooperation terms; the DOL's 2023 Wisconsin suit sought reprocessing of claims back to 2015 [theallianceorg — 2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:53:49].

sop_steps.title: Audit, market-check and file the evidence
sop_steps.action: Run the PBM fiduciary checklist on a recurring cycle and keep the output for the six-year lookback.
sop_steps.detail: Send a CAA letter on consultant compensation, audit rebates and spread pricing, and review the formulary and MAC pricing [Frier Levitt — jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:44:54]. Pair that with training, delegation, documentation, audits, market checks, RFP/RFI work and identification of every vendor fee [Seyfarth Shaw LLP — EwDJFTGZkoE @ 00:58:07].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split runs between defense-side and plaintiff-side readings of the J&J pharmacy complaint. Sam at Seyfarth Shaw rejects the plaintiffs' framing outright: pass-through-only pricing is not the legal yardstick, reasonableness is, and the headline '10 times' gap against uninsured cash prices does not by itself make a breach [EwDJFTGZkoE @ 00:31:32]. Frier Levitt's panel reads the same document as a market reset. Jonathan Levitt and Pramod John say flatly that the standard of care just went up, and Pramod expects plan sponsors to end up signing compliance attestations the way 401(k) committees and SOX filers already do [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:18:50]. On the cross-subsidy defense, the camps collide head-on. Frier Levitt predicts J&J will argue cherry-picking, offsetting rebates and plan totality, then counters that anyone claiming rebates subsidize overpriced generics has to prove it with line-level pricing [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:33:46]. Pramod's numbers push the same way: Humira nets about $30,000 to $35,000 a year after rebates, while a Cost Plus biosimilar runs about $8,400, roughly a third of that net cost [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:37:02]. Operators sitting on a PBM contract have to pick a posture before plaintiffs pick it for them: defend on aggregate reasonableness, or assume plaintiffs win the line-item fight and price every script accordingly.

Practitioners also disagree on how close the threat actually is. Mike Hill at Total Control Health Plans frames the J&J case as an awareness event rather than a wave of imminent suits, noting the class is not yet certified and the case may be dismissed [FvXAV4cqPRg @ 00:02:49]. Seyfarth's Ian builds the dismissal path in detail: standing under a Supreme Court defined-benefit pension case, cost savings that never flow dollar-for-dollar to participants, a plaintiff who did not plead she paid more, and a complaint built on 40 drugs out of thousands [EwDJFTGZkoE @ 00:39:07]. The Class Action Weekly Wire reports the opposite outcome on a health-plan theory. In the Goodyear tobacco surcharge case, plaintiffs who had actually paid the $100-a-month surcharge cleared standing on a pocketbook injury, and Judge Boyko kept the case alive past a motion to dismiss, though the 10/8 ruling was only a partial win [NtoIMU293PI @ 00:03:54]. Multnomah Group's Eric Dailey sits with the pessimists on the defense side: filing rates are high, after Northwestern the burden lies with the defense, and settlements of $8 to $15 million before fees are heading the wrong direction for fiduciary insurance [_QhwEj0_Hrg @ 00:01:39]. Plan the defense budget around the Goodyear outcome, not the hoped-for dismissal.

On governance mechanics, the playbooks diverge on how much structure a sponsor needs. Justin Burgess treats a formal committee as step one: form it, train it, document vendor selection, watch for hidden fees and bring in ERISA attorneys [Bq89alxy8qQ @ 00:00:51]. Seyfarth's Ben pushes back on rigid templates, calling his recommended practices options rather than a checklist and stating that a committee is not required [EwDJFTGZkoE @ 00:57:22]. The Alliance's John Barl lands in the middle: run an RFP to three to six vendors, score them one to ten, have a benefits committee review the spreadsheet, document why the winner won, and remember the cheapest vendor is not required [2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:37:33]. Frier Levitt attacks the scoring metric itself, arguing discount guarantees are the wrong questions to be asking and pushing item-level pricing and a non-conflicted consultant instead [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:54:25]. The practical difference is paper weight. Burgess and Barl want a documented committee trail on every vendor pick; Ben treats documentation as one tool among several, alongside training, delegation, audits, market checks and identifying every vendor fee; Frier Levitt cares less about the trail than whether the numbers being scored are the right numbers. Whichever playbook a sponsor runs, Ben's six-year lookback means the paper trail has to reach back that far.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The money trap practitioners keep hitting is the relabeled generic. Mike Hill walks the teriflunomide line from the J&J complaint: pharmacies acquire it at 91 cents per 14-milligram tablet, so a 90-day supply costs $81, yet the plan paid $10,239 for the same prescription, a 12,403% markup [FvXAV4cqPRg @ 00:02:29]. Frier Levitt explains the mechanism behind numbers like that: generics get relabeled as specialty, reimbursed at AWP minus 12% instead of AWP minus 87%, which works out to $1 to $3 a pill, and exclusivity is steered to PBM-owned specialty pharmacies [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:09:14]. Pramod John, Vivio's CEO, prices the same drug at Cost Plus at $28.40 against roughly $10,000 under the plan, about 300 times the transparent price [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:24:16]. Getting out late is expensive too, because plans that carve out specialty pay seven-figure penalties [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:38:45]. The economics check is blunt and lives in the contract. If the contract lets the PBM define what counts as a 'generic specialty' drug and route it to its own pharmacy, the overcharge hides inside a definition rather than inside the headline discount guarantee, and every renewal signed without fixing that definition stacks another year into the six-year lookback window plaintiffs use.

John Barl's contract traps at The Alliance are the most operational warnings any self-funded sponsor will hear. A handshake deal kills the exemption: without a written contract there is no ERISA 408(b)(2) protection, and prohibited transactions can carry a penalty of about 100% of the amount at issue [2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:23:16]. Leverage evaporates the moment a vendor knows it won the RFP, so limitation of liability, indemnification and data access have to sit in the RFP before anyone responds; typical vendor caps run $50,000 per error, $1 million per claim, or four times the last 12 months of fees [2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:40:26]. Lock-ins are the next trap: one year is acceptable with 60 to 90 days of termination for convenience after that, five years is risky and ten is, in Barl's words, kind of too long. The January CAA FAQ made sponsors responsible for gag clauses in downstream contracts they never see, which Barl calls a really bad result from an employer perspective [2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:51:20]. Frier Levitt shows why the data-access term is not optional: PBMs refuse to give plans their own data, and Vivio was named in the J&J complaint without ever being contacted [jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:47:45].

The administrative failures are quieter but just as expensive. In the Goodyear case, the Quit for Life program offered retroactive reimbursement, but the flyers omitted it, and the complaint alleges more than $17 million in surcharges collected from 2020 to 2025 [NtoIMU293PI @ 00:02:54]. Goodyear did win part of the fight, since collecting the surcharge was held a settlor function and plaintiffs alleged no plan loss, but the claims that survived turned on the wellness-rule disclosures. Barl's version of the same trap is eligibility drift: keep an ineligible long-term employee on the plan, let that person run up $1 million in claims, and the stop-loss carrier can deny them, which is why he wants the plan document amended and carrier sign-off obtained before covering anything outside it [2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:20:40]. On the provider side, Maritza Duran warns that TPA effective dates are staggered and can take several months, so a startup dental office can open out of network and lose visibility and foot traffic [uSNmcAr95UQ @ 00:03:46]. AHealthcareZ's economics check closes the loop: one dialysis patient costing $1 million a year equals $10 million in sales at a 10% margin, which is why report time belongs on claimants in the $20,000 to $100,000 band rather than on raw claim counts [UQkzQUPP8JE @ 00:07:19].

callout.title: Pre-Renewal Kill Switches
callout.body: These four checks map directly to the spots where practitioners watched plans leak money or land in a complaint. Clear all four before signing or renewing a PBM or TPA contract.
items: Audit every contract definition of generic, brand and specialty drug before renewal, because the J&J teriflunomide markup hid inside a definition [Total Control Health Plans — FvXAV4cqPRg @ 00:03:16].
Lock liability caps, indemnification and data access into the RFP before vendors respond, since leverage drops once the vendor knows it won [theallianceorg — 2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:40:26].
Audit retained rebates and spread at the line level, such as $1 charged to the plan versus $0.80 paid to the pharmacy [Frier Levitt — jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:58:47].
Audit the SPD and all program materials for any surcharge or wellness program so no required term goes missing from a flyer [The Class Action Weekly Wire — NtoIMU293PI @ 00:07:30].

action_checklist: Send a CAA letter demanding disclosure of consultant compensation, then audit rebates, spread pricing, the formulary and MAC pricing [Frier Levitt — jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:44:54].
Map every ERISA duty to a named owner, including who prepares, files, fixes and monitors the Form 5500, SPDs, SARs and SMMs [theallianceorg — 2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:11:14].
Run the RFP to 3 to 6 vendors with about a month to respond, score finalists 1 to 10, and document why the winner was chosen [theallianceorg — 2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:37:33].
Get item-level pricing, allow fills at Cost Plus and other pharmacies, hire a non-conflicted consultant and explore transparent models [Frier Levitt — jpLEKhmPpLs @ 00:48:19].
Require that appeals and medical necessity reviews are done by a human, because AI can be inconsistent in deciding claims [theallianceorg — 2VQyGj0Z_oY @ 00:45:28].
Pull claimant-level reports by quarter or year and aim intervention at the $20,000 to $100,000 claimant band [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — UQkzQUPP8JE @ 00:02:33].

chapters.question_prompt: How is a workers' comp experience mod calculated, and how can an employer read the worksheet and classification codes to cut premium?
chapters.title: Workers' Comp Experience Mods and Class Codes
chapters.subtitle: E-mod formula, primary and excess losses, minimum mod, experience rating worksheets, California and NCCI formula changes, and how classification codes set premium
chapters.executive_summary: Workers comp brokers, consultants, and a carrier converge on one model: the experience mod compares three of your last four years of payroll and claims against your industry's expected losses, 1.00 is average, and the factor multiplies straight against premium, turning a $100,000 standard premium into $82,000 or $122,000. They agree frequency hurts more than severity, medical-only claims enter at 30 percent, and a couple of moderate claims can flip a 0.8 to a 1.2 for three years. Street mechanics center on the minimum mod (stabilizing value over expected totals), state split points like Illinois's $30,000 with W-factor weighting, Illinois contractor's credit worth up to 40 percent, and mod and class-code audits, with one estimate that 60 to 70 percent of mods are wrong. Practitioners split on paying claims outside the system and on funding light duty.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner describes the experience mod the same way: a rating factor built specifically for your company that compares your claims against what is expected for your payroll size and industry, with 1.00 sitting at average. Gordon Coyle of The Coyle Group explains that the state rating bureau or the NCCI runs three of the last four years of payroll and claims data through its formula, producing a number like 0.82 for a credit or 1.22 for a debit [V5MJi6gMjSg @ 00:00:53]. Ryan Hanigan of JJ Doorhy & Associates frames it bluntly: under one you are better than average and earn a premium credit, over one your losses ran above what was expected and you eat a debit, and no matter which insurance company writes the policy, the same percentage gets applied [cgxTiDoClOs @ 00:01:49]. Coyle adds the system's stated purpose: charge employers with more claims than expected more, give credits to those with fewer, and use that spread as a lever to push employers toward safer workplaces [Nfw1Tq_wDio @ 00:02:14]. Jay Roberts of Wade Associates compares the mod to a credit score that pits your injury history against every competitor in your state, home builders against home builders and trucking against trucking, calling it the almighty equalizer behind massive discounts or surcharges [hX_4HXaXi4U @ 00:00:21].

The second point of agreement is that the mod is pure multiplication against your premium, so the dollar swing scales with your spend. Coyle runs two employers with the same $100,000 standard premium: the safe shop at 0.82 pays $82,000, the claims-heavy shop at 1.22 pays $122,000, a $40,000 penalty for the same payroll [V5MJi6gMjSg @ 00:01:46]. Hanigan pushes the math higher with a $500,000 manual premium, where a 0.90 mod pulls $50,000 off and a 1.10 mod adds $50,000, a $100,000 swing that lands directly on the bottom line [cgxTiDoClOs @ 00:03:15]. Ryan Stillwell of Stillwell Risk Partners pulls a real Pennsylvania bar and restaurant policy showing a 138.9 percent mod that turns $12,538 of manual premium into $17,415, nearly $5,000 extra on a twelve-thousand-dollar policy, and estimates a claim-free 0.8 would have flipped that into a $7,500 difference [tUclSqTs7E8 @ 00:03:24]. Stillwell also sets a working threshold: once workers comp premium runs past $25,000, monitoring the mod starts paying off because the multiplier effect and your control both grow. Trent Hess of BCF Group warns the move is fast and sticky: a couple of moderate claims can take a business from 0.8 to 1.2, and that hit stays for three years [c069PHgKa8Y @ 00:01:30].

The third consensus pillar is that frequency, not severity, is what wrecks a mod, and the formula is deliberately built that way. Coyle reduces the whole playbook to one line: you lower the mod by having fewer claims, period, and those claims can be controlled, though old losses stick until they flush out of the three-of-four-year window [V5MJi6gMjSg @ 00:02:58]. Hanigan says the formula refuses to punish one fluke accident, so one $50,000 claim hurts less than five $10,000 claims carrying the same total dollars, and underwriters pricing the account read frequency as the bigger red flag too [cgxTiDoClOs @ 00:13:33]. Scott Simmonds walks the actual worksheet and makes the same point with smaller numbers: five $1,200 claims hit harder than a single $7,000 claim [UkIk-T0NP3M @ 00:02:05]. Jonathan at Texas Mutual adds the second built-in discount: the NCCI formula is adjusted to lower the impact of severe and medical-only losses, so a $100 medical-only claim is cut by 70 percent and only $30 touches the emod, while some small losses never move the mod at all [gt3I3IxlEkE @ 00:01:45]. The operator takeaway everyone lands on is identical: count claims, keep them medical-only where possible, and get injured workers back on the job.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The sharpest street tool is the minimum mod, the number you would carry with zero injuries and zero claim costs. Michael Stack, CEO of Amaxx, pulls just two numbers off the NCCI rating worksheet: divide the stabilizing value by the expected totals and you have your lowest possible mod [z2GYx81GGEM @ 00:01:47]. Stack's board example takes $10 million of payroll at a 5.05 class rate, lands manual premium at $500,000, and shows a 0.8 mod producing $400,000; if the minimum is 0.4, that same premium could be $200,000, meaning the company celebrating its credit mod is paying twice what it could, and larger organizations tend to have lower minimums because of the weighting value [z2GYx81GGEM @ 00:05:12]. Jay Roberts runs a smaller version: a business paying $100,000 with a 0.91 mod whose minimum is 0.71 still has another 20 percent of room, and Roberts insists you never settle just because you are under one [dLKCbT6-S3c @ 00:01:17]. Coyle stretches it further with a $200,000 account at 1.10 and a 0.77 minimum, a 33-point spread worth at least $60,000, plus roughly $20,000 more from competitive rating tiers, which practically halves premium [njIghi8P9jQ @ 00:01:46].

The mechanic behind frequency weighting is the split point. Simmonds walks the worksheet: any loss over $5,000 carries into the actual primary losses column at only $5,000, so a $10,000 claim moves over at $5,000, and open claims count paid dollars plus reserves [UkIk-T0NP3M @ 00:03:44]. ClinardInsGroup reports the NCCI phase-in beginning in 2012, raising that $5,000 frequency cap each year until it reached $17,000 in 2015, then indexing it for inflation, so more of every loss now lands on the frequency side [-hUWvUBIr1A @ 00:01:36]. Hanigan gives current state split points of $30,000 in Illinois, $18,500 in Indiana, and $21,500 in Wisconsin: every dollar up to the split counts at 100 percent, and above it only the W factor share enters. With a W of 0.40, a $50,000 Illinois claim sends $30,000 plus $8,000 into the formula while 60 percent of the excess is thrown out [cgxTiDoClOs @ 00:15:39]. Hanigan then adds two levers that matter at the desk: medical-only claims enter at 30 cents on the dollar, so a $25,000 claim with the worker on light duty counts as $7,500, and open reserves are locked in exactly like paid dollars when loss runs go to NCCI [cgxTiDoClOs @ 00:16:45].

The payroll side of the equation gets its own street mechanics. Coyle says the business, not individual job tasks, sets the governing classification: a New York landscaper sits in 0042 for mowing, hedge trimming and planting alike, with clerical office staff split into 8810 as the common exception, and rates stack state loss costs with insurer loss cost multipliers that big carriers run in 5 to 12 tiered versions [7sfUUlxeHHk @ 00:03:54]. WorkCompConsultants counts roughly 700 codes across state rating authorities, each with its own rate, and pushes a proactive code review before an auditor finds the misclassification and bills it as large additional premium [tkOuTso-3RA @ 00:01:52]. On the mod itself, Coyle describes contingency audit consultants who look back up to three years for errors, earn refunds on prior policies, and keep 50 percent of those refunds as their fee, versus specialist brokers who verify mods for committed new clients with no fee [V5MJi6gMjSg @ 00:04:37]. Fusco On Insurance adds a timing trap: if payroll audits run late, only losses or expected losses reach the WCIRB without your payroll, making the California E-Mod look worse, so Fusco drives audits to finish on time and runs reports to check bureau data [8Reu6Q_HdTE @ 00:03:59].
